# Architect

Design before implementing. Sketch types, function signatures, class shapes, and module boundaries with `not implemented` bodies and pseudocode. Synthesize across multiple model perspectives, then fill in code against the chosen sketch. If implementation proves the sketch wrong, throw it out and redesign.

## Start

Open a todolist with one entry per phase before starting.

1. Ground
2. Sketch
3. Agree
4. Implement
5. Scrap

## Phase A: Ground the problem

Build a real mental model of every system the new code touches. Run the **how** skill over the relevant subsystems.

Naming a file isn't grounding. Produce the traced model `how` prescribes. If the design redefines ownership or layering, also run the **why** skill on the existing shape so the rationale becomes a constraint, not a guess.

Skip Phase A only when the work is genuinely greenfield with no surrounding system to integrate.

## Phase B: Sketch

Run the **arena** skill with the design-sketch task and the Phase A grounding artifacts. Send one `delegate_task` per runner, `mode: "async"`, and drain with `task_status`. Every brief stands alone: child agents get only the brief, never this thread's context. Each brief carries the task, the grounding artifacts, and `references/runner-prompt.md`. Take the runners from the `architect runners` line in `p3-models.md`, in place of the `arena runners` line. Resolve the roles against `orchestrator_capabilities`; never hardcode a model. Design it twice. Require at least two structurally distinct candidates before synthesis, even when the first looks sufficient. This is the **exhaust-the-design-space** principle skill made concrete. Whole-shape alternatives, not point fixes inside one shape.

Screen every candidate against [`references/design-red-flags.md`](references/design-red-flags.md) before synthesis. Assume the next contributor is an agent that sees only the files it opened, copies the nearest example, and takes the shortest path that compiles. Prefer the design where a change that looks right from one file is right for the whole repo.

Compare viable candidates on interface depth. Prefer the design that hides more complexity behind a smaller, simpler public surface. A rich interface can keep call chains short by concentrating capability instead of scattering it across layers.

## Phase C: Agree (opt-in)

Default: proceed directly to implementation with the synthesized design. No human checkpoint.

Opt in to a checkpoint when the invoker explicitly asks: "/architect with checkpoint," "stop and show me before implementing," or similar. Then surface the synthesized design in the thread and pause for sign-off.

The synthesis can ship as its own commit either way, as the "scaffold first" mode of the **foundational-thinking** principle skill. Planned and scoped breakage during fill-in is fine, per the **outcome-oriented-execution** principle skill. ---
name: arena
description: "Spawn N parallel candidates at the same task, pick a base, graft the strongest parts of the losers into it. Use for /arena, 'arena this', 'throw it in the arena', or when one attempt at a non-trivial artifact would lock in the wrong shape."

# Arena

Fan out N parallel attempts at the same task. Read every candidate end to end. Pick the strongest as the base. Graft the best ideas from the others into it. Verify the synthesized result.

## Start

Open a todolist with one entry per phase before launching anything.

1. Frame
2. Fan out
3. Cross-judge
4. Pick
5. Graft
6. Verify

## Phase A: Frame

The N candidates will receive the same prompt, so the prompt is the contract.

1. State the artifact each candidate is producing.
2. Derive the rubric. State what success looks like for *this* task, then turn it into 3-6 concrete gradeable criteria. The rubric is the picker's tool in Phase D. Candidates only see the task.
3. Pick the runners. Use the `arena runners` line in `p3-models.md`, resolved against `orchestrator_capabilities`. If the file or that line is missing, run `setup-p3` or pick one model per available provider from `orchestrator_capabilities`. An `auto` or `inherit-parent` entry in this line or the cross-judge line means the parent model, so omit `model` for it. If `delegate_task` rejects a configured entry, run that seat on the closest valid model of the same provider from its error message and say so. Spawn more when the arena covers multiple design directions. Same model N times when the work is generation-bound rather than judgment-sensitive.
4. Assign output paths. Each candidate writes to its own location (a git worktree where possible, otherwise `/tmp/arena-<slug>/candidate-<n>/`), per the **separate-before-serializing-shared-state** principle skill. A candidate that needs its own worktree gets one through `t3_thread_launch` with a `workspaceStrategy`. One writer per worktree.

## Phase B: Fan out

Spawn all N candidates in one turn with `delegate_task`, one per runner entry, each with `mode: "async"`. T3 child agents get only the brief, never the parent's context, so every brief stands alone: the task, the path to the shared grounding, its own output path, and instructions to produce both the artifact and a short rationale.

Each rationale names the alternatives the candidate considered and what it rejected.

Drain the candidates with `task_status`. If a candidate fails to produce output, proceed with N-1 and note the dropout in the synthesis record.

## Phase C: Cross-judge

After all Phase B candidates complete, choose one model from the `arena cross-judge pool` line in `p3-models.md`. Prefer a different provider from the parent's. Spawn one judge with `delegate_task` on that model. The brief says read-only: inspect only, no writes. It sees the rubric and the candidates by path label, scores each criterion, and recommends a base with rationale. It runs in parallel with the parent's reading in Phase D, not with the candidates themselves. Don't spawn the judge while candidates are still writing.

## Phase D: Pick a base

Read every candidate end to end before picking.

Score each candidate against the rubric criterion by criterion, not on holistic feel. Compare against the cross-judge. Agreement on the base confirms the pick. Disagreement means one of you is biased or the rubric was ambiguous. Read both rationales before deciding.

Pick the base on which candidate a future maintainer can extend most easily without breaking invariants. Prefer the cleaner boundary or smaller API when two feel tied, per the Laziness Protocol.

Record the pick and the reason in a short synthesis note alongside the base artifact, including the cross-judge's verdict.

## Phase E: Graft

Walk each losing candidate once more and identify what is worth porting into the base. The signal is usually one or two things per candidate, not most of it.

Fold each graft in by hand, per the **redesign-from-first-principles** principle skill. Don't paste mechanically. The result has to remain coherent under one mental model.

Record what was grafted, from which candidate, and what was rejected and why.

When N candidates converge on the same shape, that is a strong agreement signal. Note the convergence in the record and ship the consensus shape. No graft is needed. When N candidates wildly diverge, Phase A was under-specified. Reframe and re-run rather than averaging the divergence.

## Phase F: Verify

The synthesized artifact has to hold up under the same scrutiny as any other output, per the **prove-it-works** principle skill.

If verification surfaces a problem the arena did not catch, either Phase A was wrong (re-frame and re-run) or one candidate caught it and you missed the graft (go back to Phase E). Don't paper over.

## Outputs

One synthesized artifact. One short synthesis note alongside, naming the base, the grafts (with source candidate), the rejections, the dropouts if any, and the verification result.
# Architect runner prompt

The orchestrator passes this file through to every parallel candidate runner as its `delegate_task` brief during Phase B, filling in the variable inputs around it: the task, the Phase A grounding artifacts, the isolated working directory, and the path to write outputs. The working directory is a git worktree when available, otherwise a per-runner subdirectory under the sketch dir. What matters is independence between candidates.

You are producing one candidate design in architect's parallel exploration. Read the **architect** skill in full first. That's the workflow you're inside. Output a candidate design package: type sketch, function signatures, module map, and prose rationale shaped per [`references/rationale-template.md`](references/rationale-template.md).

Apply the following discipline. The orchestrator compares candidates on these axes to pick a base.

- Caller's usage first. Write the README-style usage and two or three real call sites before the types, then derive the type sketch from them. The usage is the spec. The two must agree, so reconcile the sketch to the usage, not the reverse.
- Data structures first. Get the core types right and the code becomes obvious. Trace each dominant access pattern through the proposed structure. If the answer is "we'll add a map / index / cache later," the structure is wrong.
- Interface depth. Compare the capability hidden behind the public surface relative to the size of that surface. Prefer a simple interface that pulls complexity into the callee, even when the implementation becomes less simple. Do not put transport or wire types on the public API. Parse into domain types behind the interface.
- Shared state: if two actors might both write, ask "what happens?" If the answer isn't "nothing," default to per-actor state with a merge at the read boundary, per the **separate-before-serializing-shared-state** principle skill.
- Make boundaries visible. `not implemented` errors for bodies, `// TODO` pseudocode for tricky logic, doc comments stating intent and invariants. A reader should trace data from input to output by reading types and signatures alone.
- Encode invariants in types: hard-to-misuse types > runtime checks > prose comments, per the **encode-lessons-in-structure** principle skill.
- Validate at boundaries, trust types inside, per the **boundary-discipline** principle skill. Business logic as pure functions. The shell stays thin.
- Single source of truth per invariant. Derive instead of sync.
- Idempotent state transitions where applicable, per the **make-operations-idempotent** principle skill. Ask what happens if the operation runs twice or crashes halfway.
- Short call chains. If tracing the flow needs more than three files, flatten the hierarchy, per the **laziness-protocol** and **minimize-reader-load** principle skills.

You are one of several runners, each on a different model. Produce the best design your model can make. Don't hedge against the others. Differences between candidates are the signal used to pick a base and graft. Converging on a safe-looking middle defeats the exploration.
# Rationale template

The prose that ships alongside the type sketch. One page. Sentence-case headings, no boilerplate. Replace the italic notes with actual content.

## Problem

*One paragraph. What we're trying to do, and what about the existing system or constraints makes the shape non-obvious. If [Phase A](../SKILL.md#phase-a-ground-the-problem) surfaced constraints the design must honor (existing types to interop with, callers we can't break, invariants that crossed our boundary), name them here so the reader sees the same constraints you saw.*

## Usage (caller's view)

*Write this first, before the type sketch. Show the README or quickstart the consumer reads, plus two or three realistic call sites in their own code. What they import, what they call, what comes back. The type sketch in [Shape](#shape) is derived from this. The two must agree. When they diverge, reconcile the sketch to the usage, not the reverse. The caller's experience is the spec. The types serve it.*

## Shape

*The recommended architecture. Data structures first. Then how data flows through the signatures. Name the load-bearing decisions. State which invariants are encoded in types, where validation lives, and what the system deliberately does not do. Judge interface depth explicitly. State what complexity the public surface hides, what remains exposed to callers, and why the interface is no larger than needed. Cite the principle behind each decision (e.g., `per boundary-discipline`). Don't restate it.*

## Synthesis decision

*Filled in by [arena](../../arena/SKILL.md). Records which candidate became the base and why, what was adapted from each of the others, and what was rejected and why.*

## Tradeoffs accepted

*One bullet per tradeoff the chosen shape makes. Form: "we accept X in exchange for Y." Name anything a future reader might mistake for an oversight, including things that look like premature optimization or premature simplification.*

## Alternatives considered

*Required. Name at least one concrete alternative shape, with one line on why it lost. Judge each alternative on interface depth, not implementation simplicity alone. Name the complexity it exposes to callers and the complexity it hides. Two or three alternatives belong here when the design space had real contenders. One is fine when the constraints forced the answer, with the conclusion phrased as "this was the only viable shape because..." Avoid listing flavors of the same shape. This section covers design alternatives the chosen shape considered and rejected, not other runner candidates.*

## Open questions and risks

*Things you noticed during the sketch that the human needs to weigh in on, and risks worth flagging before implementation starts. Phrase as questions, not assertions, so the human's answer is the resolution rather than a comment.*

## Next implementation step

*The first thing to build against the sketch. One sentence. What you'd start writing immediately after synthesis (or after Phase D sign-off, if a checkpoint was opted into).*
# Design red flags

Screen every candidate before synthesis. A red flag is a reason to revise or reject the shape.

## Shallow module

A shallow module exposes a large interface while hiding little complexity. Judge depth by the capability and policy hidden behind the public surface relative to the size of that surface. Prefer a simple interface backed by substantial behavior.

Do not confuse a deep module with a deep call chain. A deep call chain scatters understanding across layers. A deep module concentrates capability behind one interface.

Look for these signs:

- Callers coordinate several methods to complete one operation.
- Public options expose internal stages or implementation choices.
- Learning the interface does not save the caller from learning the implementation.

## Information leakage

Information leakage makes multiple modules depend on the same internal decision. A representation, policy, or protocol detail appears in more than one place, so changing it requires coordinated edits.

Public re-exports of transport or wire types are leakage. Parse external data into domain types behind the interface. Keep storage schemas, framework objects, and protocol details private.

## Temporal decomposition

Temporal decomposition organizes modules by execution order instead of the knowledge they own. Separate load, validate, transform, and save stages often repeat one representation and its invariants across several boundaries.

Group code around domain knowledge and ownership. Methods that run at different times can still belong to one module when they protect the same decisions.

## Pass-through method

A pass-through method forwards the same arguments to another method with the same shape. It adds a layer without hiding complexity.

Remove it or move responsibility to the module that can complete the operation. Keep a forwarding boundary only when it adds policy, adaptation, or a distinct abstraction.

## Split ownership

More than one module writes the same state or keeps its own copy of it. An agent that edits one writer can't see the others, so their rules diverge.

Give each piece of state one owner. Other modules read it or ask the owner to change it.

## Two ways to do one task

The design supports more than one way to do the same task. An agent copies whichever way it finds first, so every way keeps gaining callers.

Keep one way. Move callers off the others and delete them in the same change.

## Importable internals

A caller can import a module's internals. An agent takes the shortest path that compiles, so it imports them directly and they become part of the interface.

Make internals unreachable from outside the module, so an import from outside fails the build.

## Hand-synced list

Two or more places list the same items, and adding an item means editing every list. An agent that sees one list updates only that one.

Keep one list and derive the others from it. If a list can't be derived, make the build fail when the lists disagree.

# Arena

Fan out N parallel attempts at the same task. Read every candidate end to end. Pick the strongest as the base. Graft the best ideas from the others into it. Verify the synthesized result.

## Start

Open a todolist with one entry per phase before launching anything.

1. Frame
2. Fan out
3. Cross-judge
4. Pick
5. Graft
6. Verify

## Phase A: Frame

The N candidates will receive the same prompt, so the prompt is the contract.

1. State the artifact each candidate is producing.
2. Derive the rubric. State what success looks like for *this* task, then turn it into 3-6 concrete gradeable criteria. The rubric is the picker's tool in Phase D. Candidates only see the task.
3. Pick the runners. Use the `arena runners` line in `p3-models.md`, resolved against `orchestrator_capabilities`. If the file or that line is missing, run `setup-p3` or pick one model per available provider from `orchestrator_capabilities`. An `auto` or `inherit-parent` entry in this line or the cross-judge line means the parent model, so omit `model` for it. If `delegate_task` rejects a configured entry, run that seat on the closest valid model of the same provider from its error message and say so. Spawn more when the arena covers multiple design directions. Same model N times when the work is generation-bound rather than judgment-sensitive.
4. Assign output paths. Each candidate writes to its own location (a git worktree where possible, otherwise `/tmp/arena-<slug>/candidate-<n>/`), per the **separate-before-serializing-shared-state** principle skill. A candidate that needs its own worktree gets one through `t3_thread_launch` with a `workspaceStrategy`. One writer per worktree.

## Phase B: Fan out

Spawn all N candidates in one turn with `delegate_task`, one per runner entry, each with `mode: "async"`. T3 child agents get only the brief, never the parent's context, so every brief stands alone: the task, the path to the shared grounding, its own output path, and instructions to produce both the artifact and a short rationale.

Each rationale names the alternatives the candidate considered and what it rejected.

Drain the candidates with `task_status`. If a candidate fails to produce output, proceed with N-1 and note the dropout in the synthesis record.

## Phase C: Cross-judge

After all Phase B candidates complete, choose one model from the `arena cross-judge pool` line in `p3-models.md`. Prefer a different provider from the parent's. Spawn one judge with `delegate_task` on that model. The brief says read-only: inspect only, no writes. It sees the rubric and the candidates by path label, scores each criterion, and recommends a base with rationale. It runs in parallel with the parent's reading in Phase D, not with the candidates themselves. Don't spawn the judge while candidates are still writing.

## Phase D: Pick a base

Read every candidate end to end before picking.

Score each candidate against the rubric criterion by criterion, not on holistic feel. Compare against the cross-judge. Agreement on the base confirms the pick. Disagreement means one of you is biased or the rubric was ambiguous. Read both rationales before deciding.

Pick the base on which candidate a future maintainer can extend most easily without breaking invariants. Prefer the cleaner boundary or smaller API when two feel tied, per the Laziness Protocol.

Record the pick and the reason in a short synthesis note alongside the base artifact, including the cross-judge's verdict.

## Phase E: Graft

Walk each losing candidate once more and identify what is worth porting into the base. The signal is usually one or two things per candidate, not most of it.

Fold each graft in by hand, per the **redesign-from-first-principles** principle skill. Don't paste mechanically. The result has to remain coherent under one mental model.

Record what was grafted, from which candidate, and what was rejected and why.

When N candidates converge on the same shape, that is a strong agreement signal. Note the convergence in the record and ship the consensus shape. No graft is needed. When N candidates wildly diverge, Phase A was under-specified. Reframe and re-run rather than averaging the divergence.

## Phase F: Verify

The synthesized artifact has to hold up under the same scrutiny as any other output, per the **prove-it-works** principle skill.

If verification surfaces a problem the arena did not catch, either Phase A was wrong (re-frame and re-run) or one candidate caught it and you missed the graft (go back to Phase E). Don't paper over.

## Outputs

One synthesized artifact. One short synthesis note alongside, naming the base, the grafts (with source candidate), the rejections, the dropouts if any, and the verification result.

description: "Spawn N parallel candidates at the same task, pick a base, graft the strongest parts of the losers into it. Use for /arena, 'arena this', 'throw it in the arena', or when one attempt at a non-trivial artifact would lock in the wrong shape."

# Arena

Fan out N parallel attempts at the same task. Read every candidate end to end. Pick the strongest as the base. Graft the best ideas from the others into it. Verify the synthesized result.

## Start

Open a todolist with one entry per phase before launching anything.

1. Frame
2. Fan out
3. Cross-judge
4. Pick
5. Graft
6. Verify

## Phase A: Frame

The N candidates will receive the same prompt, so the prompt is the contract.

1. State the artifact each candidate is producing.
2. Derive the rubric. State what success looks like for *this* task, then turn it into 3-6 concrete gradeable criteria. The rubric is the picker's tool in Phase D. Candidates only see the task.
3. Pick the runners. Use the `arena runners` line in `p3-models.md`, resolved against `orchestrator_capabilities`. If the file or that line is missing, run `setup-p3` or pick one model per available provider from `orchestrator_capabilities`. An `auto` or `inherit-parent` entry in this line or the cross-judge line means the parent model, so omit `model` for it. If `delegate_task` rejects a configured entry, run that seat on the closest valid model of the same provider from its error message and say so. Spawn more when the arena covers multiple design directions. Same model N times when the work is generation-bound rather than judgment-sensitive.
4. Assign output paths. Each candidate writes to its own location (a git worktree where possible, otherwise `/tmp/arena-<slug>/candidate-<n>/`), per the **separate-before-serializing-shared-state** principle skill. A candidate that needs its own worktree gets one through `t3_thread_launch` with a `workspaceStrategy`. One writer per worktree.

## Phase B: Fan out

Spawn all N candidates in one turn with `delegate_task`, one per runner entry, each with `mode: "async"`. T3 child agents get only the brief, never the parent's context, so every brief stands alone: the task, the path to the shared grounding, its own output path, and instructions to produce both the artifact and a short rationale.

Each rationale names the alternatives the candidate considered and what it rejected.

Drain the candidates with `task_status`. If a candidate fails to produce output, proceed with N-1 and note the dropout in the synthesis record.

## Phase C: Cross-judge

After all Phase B candidates complete, choose one model from the `arena cross-judge pool` line in `p3-models.md`. Prefer a different provider from the parent's. Spawn one judge with `delegate_task` on that model. The brief says read-only: inspect only, no writes. It sees the rubric and the candidates by path label, scores each criterion, and recommends a base with rationale. It runs in parallel with the parent's reading in Phase D, not with the candidates themselves. Don't spawn the judge while candidates are still writing.

## Phase D: Pick a base

Read every candidate end to end before picking.

Score each candidate against the rubric criterion by criterion, not on holistic feel. Compare against the cross-judge. Agreement on the base confirms the pick. Disagreement means one of you is biased or the rubric was ambiguous. Read both rationales before deciding.

Pick the base on which candidate a future maintainer can extend most easily without breaking invariants. Prefer the cleaner boundary or smaller API when two feel tied, per the Laziness Protocol.

Record the pick and the reason in a short synthesis note alongside the base artifact, including the cross-judge's verdict.

## Phase E: Graft

Walk each losing candidate once more and identify what is worth porting into the base. The signal is usually one or two things per candidate, not most of it.

Fold each graft in by hand, per the **redesign-from-first-principles** principle skill. Don't paste mechanically. The result has to remain coherent under one mental model.

Record what was grafted, from which candidate, and what was rejected and why.

When N candidates converge on the same shape, that is a strong agreement signal. Note the convergence in the record and ship the consensus shape. No graft is needed. When N candidates wildly diverge, Phase A was under-specified. Reframe and re-run rather than averaging the divergence.

## Phase F: Verify

The synthesized artifact has to hold up under the same scrutiny as any other output, per the **prove-it-works** principle skill.

If verification surfaces a problem the arena did not catch, either Phase A was wrong (re-frame and re-run) or one candidate caught it and you missed the graft (go back to Phase E). Don't paper over.

## Outputs

One synthesized artifact. One short synthesis note alongside, naming the base, the grafts (with source candidate), the rejections, the dropouts if any, and the verification result.
# Architect runner prompt

The orchestrator passes this file through to every parallel candidate runner as its `delegate_task` brief during Phase B, filling in the variable inputs around it: the task, the Phase A grounding artifacts, the isolated working directory, and the path to write outputs. The working directory is a git worktree when available, otherwise a per-runner subdirectory under the sketch dir. What matters is independence between candidates.

You are producing one candidate design in architect's parallel exploration. Read the **architect** skill in full first. That's the workflow you're inside. Output a candidate design package: type sketch, function signatures, module map, and prose rationale shaped per [`references/rationale-template.md`](references/rationale-template.md).

Apply the following discipline. The orchestrator compares candidates on these axes to pick a base.

- Caller's usage first. Write the README-style usage and two or three real call sites before the types, then derive the type sketch from them. The usage is the spec. The two must agree, so reconcile the sketch to the usage, not the reverse.
- Data structures first. Get the core types right and the code becomes obvious. Trace each dominant access pattern through the proposed structure. If the answer is "we'll add a map / index / cache later," the structure is wrong.
- Interface depth. Compare the capability hidden behind the public surface relative to the size of that surface. Prefer a simple interface that pulls complexity into the callee, even when the implementation becomes less simple. Do not put transport or wire types on the public API. Parse into domain types behind the interface.
- Shared state: if two actors might both write, ask "what happens?" If the answer isn't "nothing," default to per-actor state with a merge at the read boundary, per the **separate-before-serializing-shared-state** principle skill.
- Make boundaries visible. `not implemented` errors for bodies, `// TODO` pseudocode for tricky logic, doc comments stating intent and invariants. A reader should trace data from input to output by reading types and signatures alone.
- Encode invariants in types: hard-to-misuse types > runtime checks > prose comments, per the **encode-lessons-in-structure** principle skill.
- Validate at boundaries, trust types inside, per the **boundary-discipline** principle skill. Business logic as pure functions. The shell stays thin.
- Single source of truth per invariant. Derive instead of sync.
- Idempotent state transitions where applicable, per the **make-operations-idempotent** principle skill. Ask what happens if the operation runs twice or crashes halfway.
- Short call chains. If tracing the flow needs more than three files, flatten the hierarchy, per the **laziness-protocol** and **minimize-reader-load** principle skills.

You are one of several runners, each on a different model. Produce the best design your model can make. Don't hedge against the others. Differences between candidates are the signal used to pick a base and graft. Converging on a safe-looking middle defeats the exploration.
# Rationale template

The prose that ships alongside the type sketch. One page. Sentence-case headings, no boilerplate. Replace the italic notes with actual content.

## Problem

*One paragraph. What we're trying to do, and what about the existing system or constraints makes the shape non-obvious. If [Phase A](../SKILL.md#phase-a-ground-the-problem) surfaced constraints the design must honor (existing types to interop with, callers we can't break, invariants that crossed our boundary), name them here so the reader sees the same constraints you saw.*

## Usage (caller's view)

*Write this first, before the type sketch. Show the README or quickstart the consumer reads, plus two or three realistic call sites in their own code. What they import, what they call, what comes back. The type sketch in [Shape](#shape) is derived from this. The two must agree. When they diverge, reconcile the sketch to the usage, not the reverse. The caller's experience is the spec. The types serve it.*

## Shape

*The recommended architecture. Data structures first. Then how data flows through the signatures. Name the load-bearing decisions. State which invariants are encoded in types, where validation lives, and what the system deliberately does not do. Judge interface depth explicitly. State what complexity the public surface hides, what remains exposed to callers, and why the interface is no larger than needed. Cite the principle behind each decision (e.g., `per boundary-discipline`). Don't restate it.*

## Synthesis decision

*Filled in by [arena](../../arena/SKILL.md). Records which candidate became the base and why, what was adapted from each of the others, and what was rejected and why.*

## Tradeoffs accepted

*One bullet per tradeoff the chosen shape makes. Form: "we accept X in exchange for Y." Name anything a future reader might mistake for an oversight, including things that look like premature optimization or premature simplification.*

## Alternatives considered

*Required. Name at least one concrete alternative shape, with one line on why it lost. Judge each alternative on interface depth, not implementation simplicity alone. Name the complexity it exposes to callers and the complexity it hides. Two or three alternatives belong here when the design space had real contenders. One is fine when the constraints forced the answer, with the conclusion phrased as "this was the only viable shape because..." Avoid listing flavors of the same shape. This section covers design alternatives the chosen shape considered and rejected, not other runner candidates.*

## Open questions and risks

*Things you noticed during the sketch that the human needs to weigh in on, and risks worth flagging before implementation starts. Phrase as questions, not assertions, so the human's answer is the resolution rather than a comment.*

## Next implementation step

*The first thing to build against the sketch. One sentence. What you'd start writing immediately after synthesis (or after Phase D sign-off, if a checkpoint was opted into).*
# Design red flags

Screen every candidate before synthesis. A red flag is a reason to revise or reject the shape.

## Shallow module

A shallow module exposes a large interface while hiding little complexity. Judge depth by the capability and policy hidden behind the public surface relative to the size of that surface. Prefer a simple interface backed by substantial behavior.

Do not confuse a deep module with a deep call chain. A deep call chain scatters understanding across layers. A deep module concentrates capability behind one interface.

Look for these signs:

- Callers coordinate several methods to complete one operation.
- Public options expose internal stages or implementation choices.
- Learning the interface does not save the caller from learning the implementation.

## Information leakage

Information leakage makes multiple modules depend on the same internal decision. A representation, policy, or protocol detail appears in more than one place, so changing it requires coordinated edits.

Public re-exports of transport or wire types are leakage. Parse external data into domain types behind the interface. Keep storage schemas, framework objects, and protocol details private.

## Temporal decomposition

Temporal decomposition organizes modules by execution order instead of the knowledge they own. Separate load, validate, transform, and save stages often repeat one representation and its invariants across several boundaries.

Group code around domain knowledge and ownership. Methods that run at different times can still belong to one module when they protect the same decisions.

## Pass-through method

A pass-through method forwards the same arguments to another method with the same shape. It adds a layer without hiding complexity.

Remove it or move responsibility to the module that can complete the operation. Keep a forwarding boundary only when it adds policy, adaptation, or a distinct abstraction.

## Split ownership

More than one module writes the same state or keeps its own copy of it. An agent that edits one writer can't see the others, so their rules diverge.

Give each piece of state one owner. Other modules read it or ask the owner to change it.

## Two ways to do one task

The design supports more than one way to do the same task. An agent copies whichever way it finds first, so every way keeps gaining callers.

Keep one way. Move callers off the others and delete them in the same change.

## Importable internals

A caller can import a module's internals. An agent takes the shortest path that compiles, so it imports them directly and they become part of the interface.

Make internals unreachable from outside the module, so an import from outside fails the build.

## Hand-synced list

Two or more places list the same items, and adding an item means editing every list. An agent that sees one list updates only that one.

Keep one list and derive the others from it. If a list can't be derived, make the build fail when the lists disagree.

Delegate one task to a T3-owned child agent/subagent of THIS thread and run it with only the supplied task prompt, without copying parent conversation history. Choose providers and models from orchestrator_capabilities, which uses the same live catalog as the composer. Prefer native subagent tools for same-provider work only when they support the chosen model. Use this for any model missing from the native tool, including same-provider work, for cross-provider work, or for explicitly T3-owned child tasks. For every T3 delegated review round, call delegate_task again with the original brief, prior findings, responses, and unresolved objections in the task prompt. Track each round by its own taskId and use a distinct clientRequestId per round, stable across retries of that round. The childThreadId is backing storage, not the target for starting another delegated review round through t3_thread_send. Provider, model, model options (see orchestrator_capabilities), runtime mode, and interaction mode inherit unless target overrides them. Prefer mode='async' for long work; mode='wait' blocks until completion or timeout. timeoutMs on mode=wait is only the parent's wait budget and does not cancel the child. waitTimedOut on that wait call means the timeout fired; keep that taskId and read status on later task_status. An async child's completion wakes this thread through a notification, steered into active turns where supported or queued otherwise, so end the turn instead of polling or spawning watchers; use task_status only when the result is needed mid-turn.

L215: # Ash
L216: 
L217: A very lightweight wrapper around Vulkan
L218: ## Overview
L219: 
L220:   * [Input] A true Vulkan API without compromises
L221:   * [Input] Convenience features without limiting functionality
L222:   * [Input] Additional type safety
L223:   * [Input] Device local function pointer loading
L224:   * [Input] No validation, everything is unsafe
L225:   * [Input] Lifetime-safety on structs created with the builder pattern
L226:   * [Input] Generated from `vk.xml`
L227:   * [Input] Support for Vulkan `1.1`, `1.2`, `1.3`, `1.4`
L228:   * [Input] `no_std` support
L229: ## ⚠️ Semver compatibility warning
L230: 
L231: The Vulkan Video bindings are experimental and still seeing breaking changes in their upstream specification, and are only provided by Ash for early adopters. All related functions and types are semver-exempt ^{cite96†1 } (we allow breaking API changes while releasing Ash with non-breaking semver bumps).
L232: 
L233: ## Features
L234: ### Explicit returns with `Result`
L235: 
L236:     // function signature
L237:     pub fn create_instance(&self,
L238:                            create_info: &vk::InstanceCreateInfo<'_>,
L239:                            allocation_callbacks: Option<&vk::AllocationCallbacks<'_>>)
L240:                            -> Result<Instance, InstanceError> { .. }
L241:     let instance = entry.create_instance(&create_info, None)
L242:         .expect("Instance creation error");
L243: ### `Vec<T>` instead of mutable slices
L244: 
L245:     pub fn get_swapchain_images(&self,
L246:                                 swapchain: vk::SwapchainKHR)
L247:                                 -> VkResult<Vec<vk::Image>>;
L248:     let present_images = swapchain_loader.get_swapchain_images_khr(swapchain).unwrap();
L249: 
L250: Note: Functions don't return `Vec<T>` if this would limit the functionality. See `p_next`.
L251: ### Slices
L252: 
L253:     pub fn cmd_pipeline_barrier(&self,
L254:                                 command_buffer: vk::CommandBuffer,
L255:                                 src_stage_mask: vk::PipelineStageFlags,
L256:                                 dst_stage_mask: vk::PipelineStageFlags,
L257:                                 dependency_flags: vk::DependencyFlags,
L258:                                 memory_barriers: &[vk::MemoryBarrier<'_>],
L259:                                 buffer_memory_barriers: &[vk::BufferMemoryBarrier<'_>],
L260:                                 image_memory_barriers: &[vk::ImageMemoryBarrier<'_>]);
L261: ### Strongly typed handles
L262: 
L263: Each Vulkan handle type is exposed as a newtyped struct for improved type safety. Null handles can be constructed with `T::null()`, and handles may be freely converted to and from `u64` with `Handle::from_raw` and `Handle::as_raw` for interop with non-Ash Vulkan code.
L264: ### Builder pattern
L265: 
L266:     let queue_info = [vk::DeviceQueueCreateInfo::default()
L267:         .queue_family_index(queue_family_index)
L268:         .queue_priorities(&priorities)];
L269: 
L270:     let device_create_info = vk::DeviceCreateInfo::default()
L271:         .queue_create_infos(&queue_info)
L272:         .enabled_extension_names(&device_extension_names_raw)
L273:         .enabled_features(&features);
L274: 
L275:     let device: Device = instance
L276:         .create_device(pdevice, &device_create_info, None)
L277:         .unwrap();
L278: ### Pointer chains
L279: Use `base.push(ext)` to insert `ext` at the front of the pointer chain attached to `base`. If `ext` already contains a valid pointer chain of its own, `unsafe`ly call `extend()` instead.
L280: 
L281:     let mut variable_pointers = vk::PhysicalDeviceVariablePointerFeatures::default();
L282:     let mut corner = vk::PhysicalDeviceCornerSampledImageFeaturesNV::default();
L283: 
L284:     let mut device_create_info = vk::DeviceCreateInfo::default()
L285:         .push(&mut corner)
L286:         .push(&mut variable_pointers);
L287: The generic argument of `.push()` only allows valid structs to extend a given struct (known as cite97†`structextends` in the Vulkan registry†registry.khronos.org , mapped to `Extends*` traits). Only structs that are listed one or more times in any `structextends` will implement a `.push()`.
L288: ### Flags and constants as associated constants
L289: 
L290:     // Bitflag
L291:     vk::AccessFlags::COLOR_ATTACHMENT_READ | vk::AccessFlags::COLOR_ATTACHMENT_WRITE
L292: 
L293:     // Constant
L294:     vk::PipelineBindPoint::GRAPHICS,
L295: ### Debug/Display for Flags
L296: 
L297:     let flag = vk::AccessFlags::COLOR_ATTACHMENT_READ
L298:             | vk::AccessFlags::COLOR_ATTACHMENT_WRITE;
L299:     println!("Debug: {:?}", flag);
L300:     println!("Display: {}", flag);
L301:     // Prints:
L302:     // Debug: AccessFlags(110000000)
L303:     // Display: COLOR_ATTACHMENT_READ | COLOR_ATTACHMENT_WRITE
L304: ### Function pointer loading
L305: 
L306: Ash also takes care of loading the function pointers. Function pointers are split into 3 categories.
L307: 
L308:   * Entry: Loads the Vulkan library. Needs to outlive `Instance` and `Device`.
L309:   * Instance: Loads instance level functions. Needs to outlive the `Device`s it has created.
L310:   * Device: Loads device local functions.
L311: 
L312: The loader is just one possible implementation:
L313:   * Device level functions are retrieved on a per device basis.
L314:   * Everything is loaded by default, functions that failed to load are initialized to a function that always panics.
L315:   * Do not call Vulkan 1.1 functions if you have created a 1.0 instance. Doing so will result in a panic.
L316: 
L317: Custom loaders can be implemented.
L318: ### Extension loading
L319: 
L320: Additionally, every Vulkan extension has to be loaded explicitly. You can find all extensions directly under `ash::*` in a module with their prefix (e.g. `khr` or `ext`).
L321: 
L322:     use ash::khr;
L323:     let swapchain_loader = khr::swapchain::Device::new(&instance, &device);
L324:     let swapchain = swapchain_loader.create_swapchain(&swapchain_create_info).unwrap();
L325: ### Raw function pointers
L326: 
L327: Raw function pointers are available, if something hasn't been exposed yet in the higher level API. Please open an issue if anything is missing.
L328: 
L329:     device.fp_v1_0().destroy_device(...);
L330: ### Support for extension names
L331: 
L332:     use ash::{ext, khr};
L333:     #[cfg(all(unix, not(target_os = "android")))]
L334:     fn extension_names() -> Vec<*const i8> {
L335:         vec![
L336:             khr::surface::NAME.as_ptr(),
L337:             khr::xlib_surface::NAME.as_ptr(),
L338:             ext::debug_utils::NAME.as_ptr(),
L339:         ]
L340:     }

# Effects in Bend

An AI wrote this text from the runtime's source (`bend2/comp.ts` and
`bend2/effs/`). A human will revise it later. Report anything wrong on
GitHub.

## An effect def

An effect is a def of type `IO(R)` whose body is two imports:

```python
def Clock.now() -> IO(U32):
  import "./clock.c"
  import "./clock.js"
```

Each file registers the effect under its def with `io_eff(CID(Clock.now),
..)`. The `.c` file serves `bend x.bend -o x`; the `.js` file
serves `bend x.bend -o x.js` and `bend x.bend`. Every effect in Base is
built this way: `bend2/effs/*.c` and `*.js` are the reference.

## The C side

The compiler splices your `.c` into the program's C source after the
runtime, so every runtime symbol is in scope. Define the effect and
register it in a constructor:

```c
Term clock_now_run(Env e, Term* f, IoWork* w);

static void __attribute__((constructor)) clock_now_use(void) {
  io_eff(CID(Clock.now), clock_now_run);
}
```

`CID(Name)` is the C id of a constructor or of an effect def: the compiler
replaces it with the name's own id, reading `Name` in the effect's
namespace first (the file that declares the def), then in Base's, as the
def's body would. A constructor the program does not use has no id, so
`#ifdef CID(Name)` tests for it. `FID(name)` is a def's function id the
same way. `f` holds the def's arguments in order: a `U32` is the word
(`(u32)f[0]`), a `String` is taken with `io_cstr(e, f[0], &len)` (a
`malloc`ed copy you free), a handle with `io_hand_v(f[0])`. The loop
calls the effect at once; an effect that waits (for a handle, or for time)
parks itself, as below.

The effect returns a Term: a `U32` is `(Term)n`, `Unit` is
`term_pak(CID(Unit), 0)`, a `String` is `io_str(e, p, n)`, a two-field
constructor is `io_node(e, CID(K), a, b)`. A `Result` is `io_done(e, v)`
or `io_fail(e, code, text)` (`text` NULL prints `strerror(code)`).
`io_sys_end(w, n)` stores `errno` in `w->code` when a call fails.

A handle is a descriptor or pointer packed in one word by `io_hand(v)`. Its
type must be one of Base's handle laws (`File`, `Socket`, ...): a user
handle type is a WONTFIX entry for now, see `WONTFIX.txt`. An effect on a
handle hands it back beside its result: `io_tup(e, io_hand(h), r)`, also
on failure.

Blocking work leaves the loop in two ways. `io_work(w, call, pack)` runs
`call(w)` on a helper thread, then `pack(e, w)` on the loop; `pack`'s value
is the answer. `call` has no `Env`: it may only touch `w`.
`io_wait_on(w, fd, POLLIN, 0, more)` parks until `fd` is ready (`POLLIN` or
`POLLOUT`), then runs `more(e, w)` on the loop; `more` may call
`io_wait_on` again. Both return `IO_PARK`, which the effect returns.
Replace `0` with an absolute `io_tick()` deadline to also wake on time;
with no events (`io_wait_on(w, 0, 0, deadline, more)`) it waits on time
alone, as `sleep.c` does. An effect that can meet a steady backlog (an
accept, a datagram recv) parks before its first try, as `tcp_accept.c`
does: one that answers at once never lets the loop poll, so the backlog
would starve its timers.

`w` is the effect's scratch space: `hand`, `made`, `size`, `data`, `text`,
`code`, and `word` until it parks (`io_wait_on` keeps its fd there). The
runtime owns `w` and `f`. The effect owns `w->data`:
allocate it in the run function and free it in `pack`. In `bend2/effs/`,
`file_read.c` is the pattern for `io_work` and `tcp_recv.c` for `io_wait_on`.

## The JS side

The `.js` file is a plain script, run once in a closure of its own, that
registers the effect: `io_eff(CID(Clock.now), clock_now)`. The effect
takes the def's arguments as JS values: a `U32` is a number, a `Nat` a
number, a `String` a string, a constructor
`{$: CID(Name), field: value}`, a handle its host value (a descriptor).
`CID(Name)` is the constructor's tag, read as on the C side. It returns
the answer the same way: `io_done(v)`, `io_fail(code)`,
`io_tup(handle, result)`, `{$: CID(Unit)}`. A `Nat` answer that is not a
whole number from 0 to 2^53 stops the run; a `Nat` inside an answer goes
unchecked, so the host keeps it in that range.

A blocking effect takes one more argument, `k`, and parks with
`io_park_on(fd, out, k, more)`: it returns `undefined`, and the loop calls
`more()` when `fd` is ready; `more` answers the value, or `undefined` to
park again. Add an absolute `performance.now()` deadline as a fifth
argument to also wake on time; with no fd
(`io_park_on(undefined, false, k, more, deadline)`) it waits on time
alone, as `sleep.js` does. An effect that can meet a steady backlog
parks before its first try, as on the C side. `io_sys()` is `libc` through `bun:ffi`
(`read`, `recv`, `select`, `errno`); `tcp_accept.js` shows the full shape.

## A complete example

`main.bend`:

```python
import Base

def Clock.now() -> IO(U32):
  import "./clock.c"
  import "./clock.js"

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    t : U32 <- Clock.now()
    IO.print("ms since boot: " ++ U32.show(t))
```

`clock.c`:

```c
Term clock_now_run(Env e, Term* f, IoWork* w) {
  return (Term)(uint32_t)(io_tick() / 1000000ull);
}

static void __attribute__((constructor)) clock_now_use(void) {
  io_eff(CID(Clock.now), clock_now_run);
}
```

`clock.js`:

```js
function clock_now() {
  return Math.floor(performance.now()) >>> 0;
}

io_eff(CID(Clock.now), clock_now);
```

`bend main.bend -o main && ./main` prints a line; so do `bend main.bend -o
main.js && bun main.js` and `bend main.bend`. The output name must not be
one of the effect's files.

## Compatibility

The C side tracks the exact compiler version: the names above are the
runtime's internals, and a release may rename any of them. There is no ABI
promise. Rebuild your effects with every update.

---
name: principle-build-the-lever
description: "Apply to any non-trivial work, not just bulk work: edits, migrations, analyses, checks. Build the tool that does it or proves it (codemod, script, generator, or a skill your subagents follow) instead of working by hand. The tool is the artifact a reviewer can rerun."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Build the Lever

When the work isn't trivial, build the tool that does it instead of doing it by hand.

**Why:** Two payoffs. Throughput: a codemod, generator, or script does the work the same way every time and reruns for free. Confidence: the tool is one artifact a reviewer can read and rerun to check the work. Hand-done changes can only be re-verified by redoing them. A deterministic script turns "trust me" into "run this".

**Pattern:** Default to building the lever. Skip it only when the task is trivial, a couple of obvious edits you can see at a glance.

- Do the first unit by hand to learn the recipe, then build the tool. Prove it by rerunning it on that unit and diffing against your hand-done version. Make the lever safe to rerun.

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: src/core.bend
+import Base
+import ../deps/bend-collections/src/math/u64.bend as W
+
+def DeviceSize() -> Data:
+  W.U64
+
+def size_words(value: W.U64) -> U32 & U32:
+  W.U64{lo, hi} = value
+  (lo, hi)
+
+def size_from_words(words: U32 & U32) -> W.U64:
+  (lo, hi) = words
+  W.U64{lo, hi}
+
+def whole_size() -> W.U64:
+  W.U64{4294967295, 4294967295}
+
+def make_api_version(variant: U32, major: U32, minor: U32, patch: U32) -> U32:
+  U32.or(U32.shln(variant, 29n), U32.or(U32.shln(major, 22n), U32.or(U32.shln(minor, 12n), patch)))
+
+def api_version_major(version: U32) -> U32:
+  U32.and(U32.shrn(version, 22n), 127)
+
+def api_version_minor(version: U32) -> U32:
+  U32.and(U32.shrn(version, 12n), 1023)
+
+def api_version_patch(version: U32) -> U32:
+  U32.and(version, 4095)
+
+def flags_contains(+flags: U32, +required: U32) -> Bool:
+  U32.is_eq(U32.and(flags, required), required)
+
+type MemoryType is Data:
+  MemoryType{property_flags: U32, heap_index: U32}
+
+def memory_type_step(rest: List<MemoryType>, +bits: U32, +required: U32, +index: U32, fits: Bool) -> Maybe<U32>:
+  match fits:
+    case True{}:
+      Some{index}
+    case False{}:
+      memory_type_go(rest, U32.shr(bits), required, U32.inc(index))
+
+def memory_type_go(types: List<MemoryType>, +bits: U32, +required: U32, +index: U32) -> Maybe<U32>:
+  match types:
+    case Nil{}:
+      None{}
+    case Con{MemoryType{flags, heap}, rest}:
+      memory_type_step(rest, bits, required, index,
+        Bool.and(U32.is_ne(U32.and(bits, 1), 0), flags_contains(flags, required)))
+
+def find_memory_type(types: List<MemoryType>, bits: U32, required: U32) -> Maybe<U32>:
+  memory_type_go(types, bits, required, 0)
+
+def queue_step(rest: List<U32 & U32>, +required: U32, +index: U32, fits: Bool) -> Maybe<U32>:
+  match fits:
+    case True{}:
+      Some{index}
+    case False{}:
+      queue_go(rest, required, U32.inc(index))
+
+def queue_go(families: List<U32 & U32>, +required: U32, +index: U32) -> Maybe<U32>:
+  match families:
+    case Nil{}:
+      None{}
+    case Con{(flags, count), rest}:
+      queue_step(rest, required, index,
+        Bool.and(U32.is_ne(count, 0), flags_contains(flags, required)))
+
+def find_queue_family(families: List<U32 & U32>, required: U32) -> Maybe<U32>:
+  queue_go(families, required, 0)
*** End Patch"));

# Bend Vulkan: checked tokens and explicit dispatch

## Usage (caller's view)

The first release supports Linux Vulkan 1.0 discovery, logical devices, buffers, allocation, binding, and coherent host mapping. It keeps ash's Entry/Instance/Device division. It does not claim rendering or GPU execution support.
The following are call-site pseudocode. `checked` means matching `Done` or returning `Fail` from the callback. These are not executable Bend examples.

```text
import ./src/vulkan.bend as Vk
import ./deps/bend-collections/src/math/u64.bend as W
# Discovery callback passed to Entry.with; the helper always closes its entry.
instance = checked(Entry.create_instance(entry, InstanceInfo.default()))
devices = checked(Instance.enumerate_physical_devices(instance))
properties = checked(Instance.physical_device_properties(instance, physical))
# physical comes from devices; an empty list is a valid discovery result.
```

```text
# Allocation callback; queue family and memory types come from physical-device queries.
device = checked(Instance.create_device(instance, physical, DeviceInfo{family, 1}))
buffer = checked(Device.create_buffer(device, BufferInfo{W.U64{4096, 0}, transfer_src}))
requirements = checked(Device.buffer_memory_requirements(device, buffer))
index = checked(Memory.choose_type(memory_types, requirements.type_bits, host_visible_coherent))
memory = checked(Device.allocate_memory(device, AllocateInfo{requirements.size, index}))
checked(Device.bind_buffer_memory(device, buffer, memory, W.zero()))
mapping = checked(Device.map_memory(device, memory, W.zero(), requirements.size))
checked(Mapping.write_bytes(mapping, W.zero(), [0, 127, 255]))
bytes = checked(Mapping.read_bytes(mapping, W.zero(), 3)) # require exactly [0, 127, 255]
checked(Device.unmap_memory(device, mapping))
checked(Device.destroy_buffer(device, buffer)); checked(Device.free_memory(device, memory))
checked(Instance.destroy_device(instance, device)); checked(Entry.destroy_instance(entry, instance))
```

Each callback returns `IO(VkResult<A>)`. `Entry.with` handles cleanup after either result. Every operation above also works without that helper, with explicit `Entry.close`.

## Problem

Bend 2.0.37 supports custom effects but cannot introduce opaque foreign handle types. Constructors can carry identifiers, but callers can construct identifiers themselves. The C boundary must validate those identifiers before touching driver objects. Affine values can also be dropped, so `Type` alone cannot promise resource destruction.
Use the required [bend-collections U64](https://github.com/Giulio2002/bend-collections/blob/main/src/math/u64.bend), pinned to commit `bc78c4f4cabb536a2a1dd6e308b6a8f0afafda7c`. Import its `W.U64{lo: U32, hi: U32}` directly. Do not create another integer implementation.

## Shape

The sketch uses `VkResult<A>` as shorthand for `Result<&1, &1, Error, A>` and `Bytes` for `List<&2, U32>`. Each signature names the intended contract, with implementation bodies omitted.

```text
type Entry is Data: Entry{id: W.U64}
type Instance is Data: Instance{id: W.U64}
type PhysicalDevice is Data: PhysicalDevice{id: W.U64}
type Device is Data: Device{id: W.U64}
type Buffer is Data: Buffer{id: W.U64}
type DeviceMemory is Data: DeviceMemory{id: W.U64}
type Mapping is Data: Mapping{id: W.U64}
type ErrorKind is Data: Vulkan{} | Loader{} | InvalidHandle{} | InvalidConfig{} | Unsupported{} | Cleanup{}
type Error is Data: Error{kind: ErrorKind, code: U32, operation: String, detail: String}
type InstanceInfo is Data: InstanceInfo{application: String, api_version: U32, layers: +List<String>, extensions: +List<String>}
type DeviceInfo is Data: DeviceInfo{queue_family: U32, queue_count: U32}
type BufferUsage is Data: BufferUsage{bits: U32}
type MemoryFlags is Data: MemoryFlags{bits: U32}
type BufferInfo is Data: BufferInfo{size: W.U64, usage: BufferUsage}
type AllocateInfo is Data: AllocateInfo{size: W.U64, memory_type_index: U32}
type MemoryRequirements is Data: MemoryRequirements{size: W.U64, alignment: W.U64, type_bits: U32}
Entry.load() -> IO(VkResult<Entry>)
Entry.with(-A: Type, body: Entry -> IO(VkResult<A>)) -> IO(VkResult<A>)
Entry.create_instance(entry: Entry, info: InstanceInfo) -> IO(VkResult<Instance>)
Instance.enumerate_physical_devices(instance: Instance) -> IO(VkResult<List<PhysicalDevice>>)
Instance.physical_device_properties(instance: Instance, physical: PhysicalDevice) -> IO(VkResult<PhysicalDeviceProperties>)
Instance.queue_family_properties(instance: Instance, physical: PhysicalDevice) -> IO(VkResult<List<QueueFamilyProperties>>)
Instance.memory_properties(instance: Instance, physical: PhysicalDevice) -> IO(VkResult<MemoryProperties>)
Instance.create_device(instance: Instance, physical: PhysicalDevice, info: DeviceInfo) -> IO(VkResult<Device>)
Device.create_buffer(device: Device, info: BufferInfo) -> IO(VkResult<Buffer>)
Device.buffer_memory_requirements(device: Device, buffer: Buffer) -> IO(VkResult<MemoryRequirements>)
Memory.choose_type(types: List<MemoryType>, allowed: U32, flags: MemoryFlags) -> VkResult<U32>
Device.allocate_memory(device: Device, info: AllocateInfo) -> IO(VkResult<DeviceMemory>)
Device.bind_buffer_memory(device: Device, buffer: Buffer, memory: DeviceMemory, offset: W.U64) -> IO(VkResult<Unit>)
Device.map_memory(device: Device, memory: DeviceMemory, offset: W.U64, size: W.U64) -> IO(VkResult<Mapping>)
Mapping.write_bytes(mapping: Mapping, offset: W.U64, bytes: Bytes) -> IO(VkResult<Unit>)
Mapping.read_bytes(mapping: Mapping, offset: W.U64, count: U32) -> IO(VkResult<Bytes>)
```

Query records contain named Vulkan fields, including device name/type/API version, queue counts/flags, and memory types/heaps with U64 heap sizes. Include `InstanceInfo.default() -> InstanceInfo`. The cleanup calls shown in usage and `Entry.close(entry)` all return `IO(VkResult<Unit>)`.
Data wrappers allow normal Bend reuse through `+` bindings without threading an owner through every query. Distinct constructor types catch accidental handle mixing. C enforces liveness, parentage, and state, per boundary-discipline. The interface hides dispatch loading, allocation of query arrays, constructor marshalling, and host pointer access. Vulkan resource selection remains explicit.

## Ownership and FFI

The native registry stores a tagged union of actual `VkInstance`, `VkPhysicalDevice`, `VkDevice`, `VkBuffer`, `VkDeviceMemory`, or mapping records. Each slot records its generation and parent token. Encode tokens as `U64{slot, generation}`. Reserve zero, retire a slot before generation wrap, and bound-check before indexing. Never cast a token to a pointer or Vulkan handle. Public constructors are not an access-control boundary.
Every operation checks the token's generation, kind, complete ancestor chain, and required common parent. Repeated queries intern physical devices by instance and actual handle. Physical devices are borrowed records invalidated with their instance. Registry entries retain their parent chain and library lifetime until destruction. Invalid identifiers return `InvalidHandle` before any driver call.
`Entry` owns `dlopen("libvulkan.so.1")` and global function pointers. Each instance owns a table resolved through `vkGetInstanceProcAddr`; each device owns one resolved through `vkGetDeviceProcAddr`. Check required symbols before publishing a token. Keep the loader open until all instances and devices are destroyed. This follows [Vulkan dispatch rules](https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/vkGetInstanceProcAddr.html).
Raw effects have normal constructor arguments and `IO(Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, A>)` results. Each imports `./native.c` and `./native.js`. C uses `io_node` for U64 and wrapper constructors, `io_done` and `io_fail` for results, and `io_cstr` for copied strings. Register reachable effects with `io_eff(CID(Raw.entry_load), entry_load_run, 0)`. Guard each registration with its `CID` and guard shared C definitions against duplicate inclusion. Never use `io_hand` or invent a foreign handle law.
Generated Bend wrappers decode raw errors into `Error`. Preserve Vulkan result bits exactly as U32, and render their signed value when displaying them. Reserve a disjoint positive code range for wrapper errors and have generation reject collisions with Vulkan result values. Include the failing command and retain unknown VkResult values. Enumeration handles `VK_INCOMPLETE` with bounded retries and an explicit error on exhaustion. Never substitute errno for VkResult.
Reconstruct each size with `((uint64_t)hi << 32) | lo`, and split results in reverse. Use `VkDeviceSize` throughout size, offset, alignment, and bounds calculations. Validate overflow before addition, narrowing to `size_t`, allocation, or pointer arithmetic. Read counts are bounded U32 chunks; offsets and allocations retain all 64 bits. Never use the dependency's signed comparison for unsigned sizes.
Mapping records keep C pointers plus allocation, offset, and length. Copy operations validate byte values and the requested interval before access. Initially accept only HOST_VISIBLE | HOST_COHERENT memory for mapping; reject noncoherent mapping explicitly until flush/invalidate support exists. Reject zero sizes, double mapping, rebinding, invalid memory-type selection, and invalid alignment. Check bind requirements against actual registry metadata, following [vkBindBufferMemory](https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/vkBindBufferMemory.html).
All native operations run synchronously as sequential IO effects on the event-loop thread. The registry has one writer. No Vulkan call enters Bend's pure parallel evaluation or `IO.spawn`. Parallelize independent pure device scoring, payload preparation, and generated-file computations when the work is large enough.

## Cleanup and limited scope

Register resources only after Vulkan creation and required dispatch loading succeed. Roll back unpublished native objects on every later failure. Public destroy/free operations reject live dependents and invalidate tokens after destruction. A duplicate destroy returns `InvalidHandle`; it never reaches Vulkan twice. Dropping a Data wrapper does not destroy its object.
`Entry.close` is the explicit subtree cleanup operation used by `Entry.with`. Unmap mappings, destroy buffers, free memory, destroy devices, invalidate physical-device records, destroy instances, then close the loader. Continue cleanup after an error, including device loss, and retain diagnostics. A callback failure stays the primary error with cleanup diagnostics appended; a successful callback plus cleanup failure returns `Cleanup`. Close also invalidates every escaped token. Process termination is outside the callback cleanup guarantee.
The seed accepts exclusive non-sparse buffers, null allocators, no enabled device features/extensions, and null pNext chains. Instance layer/extension names are explicit and checked, including embedded NUL rejection. It exposes wait-idle and destroys only resources it created. It does not support native handle adoption, arbitrary pointers, callbacks, surfaces, swapchains, command submission, or shader execution. JavaScript returns an explicit native-backend-required error.

## Module map and generated growth

`src/vulkan.bend` provides typed public operations and cleanup helpers. `src/types.bend` holds checked configs, errors, and wrapper types. `src/raw.bend` declares effects; `src/native.c` owns the loader, registry, and marshalling. `src/native.js` registers clear unsupported results. `src/generated/vk.bend` contains selected constants and query records; `src/generated/dispatch.inc` contains PFN tables and loaders.
`tools/generate.py` reads a pinned Khronos `vk.xml` plus `bindings.json`, an allowlist with marshalling and lifecycle policies. Emit supported declarations and dispatch metadata deterministically. Record registry hash, Vulkan header version, and generator command. Reject unsupported pointer shapes instead of generating placeholders. The seed covers only the operations above; add a command by adding its policy and native behavior, then regenerating. Do not pretend that XML alone supplies lifetime or pointer safety.
`examples/discover.bend`, `examples/buffer_roundtrip.bend`, and `tests/native.bend` use the public API. `LAWS.bend` states pure rules. `PROOF.bend` imports and proves those rules. Pin Bend 2.0.37 because its effect ABI is internal, and compile a constructor/IO smoke test before adding Vulkan calls. The local compiler source confirms the three-argument registration although `bend guide effects` still shows two.

## Verification

Prove unsigned limb ordering, checked range inclusion, and memory-type selection soundness in `LAWS.bend`/`PROOF.bend`. Test C limb conversion with `0`, `2^32`, a mixed high/low pattern, and `2^64-1`; this is ABI evidence, not a Bend proof about foreign code. Run `bend PROOF.bend` before every commit. Native checks build with `bend examples/buffer_roundtrip.bend -o /tmp/vulkan-roundtrip`, then run that binary. The default Bend execution path is JavaScript.
Use the actual Vulkan loader and an available GPU or software ICD. Require discovery, device creation, buffer allocation/binding, mapping, exact byte roundtrip, and clean teardown. Explicitly report this as host access to Vulkan memory, without claiming GPU work. Test fabricated/stale/wrong-parent tokens, mapping bounds, failed creation rollback, and cleanup with live children. Missing an ICD is a reported integration skip, never a fabricated success. Run validation layers when available and verify the generator produces no diff on a second run.

## Tradeoffs accepted and alternatives considered

We accept registry lookups and explicit lifetime errors for constructor-compatible FFI and protection against pointer forgery. We accept a bounded supported subset and copy-based mapped access for a usable first release with clear extension points. Raw pointer-valued U64 handles lose because forged constructors could crash the driver. Affine Type contexts with state returned on every branch expose more ownership plumbing while still allowing drops and fabricated constructors. A monolithic `run_demo` effect hides Vulkan resource decisions and cannot grow into ash-like bindings.

## Open questions, synthesis, and next step

Can CI provide a software ICD and validation layers so native behavior is required on at least one runner? The orchestrator chooses the synthesis; this candidate recommends reusable checked tokens with explicit dispatch and subtree cleanup. Start by compiling the ordinary-constructor roundtrip effect and checking forged-token rejection before implementing Entry loading.

## Usage (caller's view)

The first release supports Linux Vulkan 1.0 discovery, logical devices, buffers, allocation, binding, and coherent host mapping. It keeps ash's Entry/Instance/Device division. It does not claim rendering or GPU execution support.
The following are call-site pseudocode. `checked` means matching `Done` or returning `Fail` from the callback. These are not executable Bend examples.

```text
import ./src/vulkan.bend as Vk
import ./deps/bend-collections/src/math/u64.bend as W
# Discovery callback passed to Entry.with; the helper always closes its entry.
instance = checked(Entry.create_instance(entry, InstanceInfo.default()))
devices = checked(Instance.enumerate_physical_devices(instance))
properties = checked(Instance.physical_device_properties(instance, physical))
# physical comes from devices; an empty list is a valid discovery result.
```

```text
# Allocation callback; queue family and memory types come from physical-device queries.
device = checked(Instance.create_device(instance, physical, DeviceInfo{family, 1}))
buffer = checked(Device.create_buffer(device, BufferInfo{W.U64{4096, 0}, transfer_src}))
requirements = checked(Device.buffer_memory_requirements(device, buffer))
index = checked(Memory.choose_type(memory_types, requirements.type_bits, host_visible_coherent))
memory = checked(Device.allocate_memory(device, AllocateInfo{requirements.size, index}))
checked(Device.bind_buffer_memory(device, buffer, memory, W.zero()))
mapping = checked(Device.map_memory(device, memory, W.zero(), requirements.size))
checked(Mapping.write_bytes(mapping, W.zero(), [0, 127, 255]))
bytes = checked(Mapping.read_bytes(mapping, W.zero(), 3)) # require exactly [0, 127, 255]
checked(Device.unmap_memory(device, mapping))
checked(Device.destroy_buffer(device, buffer)); checked(Device.free_memory(device, memory))
checked(Instance.destroy_device(instance, device)); checked(Entry.destroy_instance(entry, instance))
```

Each callback returns `IO(VkResult<A>)`. `Entry.with` handles cleanup after either result. Every operation above also works without that helper, with explicit `Entry.close`.

Bend 2.0.37 supports custom effects but cannot introduce opaque foreign handle types. Constructors can carry identifiers, but callers can construct identifiers themselves. The C boundary must validate those identifiers before touching driver objects. Affine values can also be dropped, so `Type` alone cannot promise resource destruction.

type Entry is Data: Entry{id: W.U64}
type Instance is Data: Instance{id: W.U64}
type PhysicalDevice is Data: PhysicalDevice{id: W.U64}
type Device is Data: Device{id: W.U64}
type Buffer is Data: Buffer{id: W.U64}
type DeviceMemory is Data: DeviceMemory{id: W.U64}
type Mapping is Data: Mapping{id: W.U64}
type ErrorKind is Data: Vulkan{} | Loader{} | InvalidHandle{} | InvalidConfig{} | Unsupported{} | Cleanup{}
type Error is Data: Error{kind: ErrorKind, code: U32, operation: String, detail: String}
type InstanceInfo is Data: InstanceInfo{application: String, api_version: U32, layers: +List<String>, extensions: +List<String>}
type DeviceInfo is Data: DeviceInfo{queue_family: U32, queue_count: U32}
type BufferUsage is Data: BufferUsage{bits: U32}
type MemoryFlags is Data: MemoryFlags{bits: U32}
type BufferInfo is Data: BufferInfo{size: W.U64, usage: BufferUsage}
type AllocateInfo is Data: AllocateInfo{size: W.U64, memory_type_index: U32}
type MemoryRequirements is Data: MemoryRequirements{size: W.U64, alignment: W.U64, type_bits: U32}

Entry.with(-A: Type, body: Entry -> IO(VkResult<A>)) -> IO(VkResult<A>)
Entry.create_instance(entry: Entry, info: InstanceInfo) -> IO(VkResult<Instance>)

Instance.queue_family_properties(instance: Instance, physical: PhysicalDevice) -> IO(VkResult<List<QueueFamilyProperties>>)
Instance.memory_properties(instance: Instance, physical: PhysicalDevice) -> IO(VkResult<MemoryProperties>)
Instance.create_device(instance: Instance, physical: PhysicalDevice, info: DeviceInfo) -> IO(VkResult<Device>)
Device.create_buffer(device: Device, info: BufferInfo) -> IO(VkResult<Buffer>)
Device.buffer_memory_requirements(device: Device, buffer: Buffer) -> IO(VkResult<MemoryRequirements>)
Memory.choose_type(types: List<MemoryType>, allowed: U32, flags: MemoryFlags) -> VkResult<U32>
Device.allocate_memory(device: Device, info: AllocateInfo) -> IO(VkResult<DeviceMemory>)
Device.bind_buffer_memory(device: Device, buffer: Buffer, memory: DeviceMemory, offset: W.U64) -> IO(VkResult<Unit>)
Device.map_memory(device: Device, memory: DeviceMemory, offset: W.U64, size: W.U64) -> IO(VkResult<Mapping>)
Mapping.write_bytes(mapping: Mapping, offset: W.U64, bytes: Bytes) -> IO(VkResult<Unit>)
Mapping.read_bytes(mapping: Mapping, offset: W.U64, count: U32) -> IO(VkResult<Bytes>)

Public constructors are not an access-control boundary.

`Entry` owns `dlopen("libvulkan.so.1")` and global function pointers. Each instance owns a table resolved through `vkGetInstanceProcAddr`; each device owns one resolved through `vkGetDeviceProcAddr`. Check required symbols before publishing a token. Keep the loader open until all instances and devices are destroyed. This follows [Vulkan dispatch rules](https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/vkGetInstanceProcAddr.html).
Raw effects have normal constructor arguments and `IO(Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, A>)` results. Each imports `./native.c` and `./native.js`. Never use the dependency's signed comparison for unsigned sizes.
Mapping records keep C pointers plus allocation, offset, and length. Copy operations validate byte values and the requested interval before access. Initially accept only HOST_VISIBLE | HOST_COHERENT memory for mapping; reject noncoherent mapping explicitly until flush/invalidate support exists. Check bind requirements against actual registry metadata, following [vkBindBufferMemory](https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/vkBindBufferMemory.html).
All native operations run synchronously as sequential IO effects on the event-loop thread. The registry has one writer. No Vulkan call enters Bend's pure parallel evaluation or `IO.spawn`. Parallelize independent pure device scoring, payload preparation, and generated-file computations when the work is large enough.

A monolithic `run_demo` effect hides Vulkan resource decisions and cannot grow into ash-like bindings.

+import Base

+type Entry is Data:

+type Instance is Data:
+  Instance{key: U32}
+type PhysicalDevice is Data:
+  PhysicalDevice{key: U32}

+type DeviceMemory is Data:
+  DeviceMemory{key: U32}
+type CommandPool is Data:
+  CommandPool{key: U32}
+type CommandBuffer is Data:
+  CommandBuffer{key: U32}
+
+type InstanceCreateInfo is Type:
+  InstanceCreateInfo{application_name: String, api_version: U32, layers: List<String>, extensions: List<String>}
+
+def InstanceCreateInfo.default() -> InstanceCreateInfo:
+  InstanceCreateInfo{"Bend Vulkan", Core.make_api_version(0, 1, 0, 0), [], []}
+
+type DeviceCreateInfo is Type:
+  DeviceCreateInfo{queue_family_index: U32, extensions: List<String>}
+
+type BufferCreateInfo is Data:
+  BufferCreateInfo{size: W.U64, usage: U32}
+
+type PhysicalDeviceProperties is Data:
+  PhysicalDeviceProperties{device_name: String, api_version: U32, driver_version: U32, vendor_id: U32, device_id: U32, device_type: U32}
+
+type MemoryRequirements is Data:
+  MemoryRequirements{size: W.U64, alignment: W.U64, memory_type_bits: U32}
+
+# Negative VkResult values retain their exact two's-complement U32 bits.
+# Wrapper failures occupy 0x60000000..0x600000ff and include a message.
+def VkResult(-A: Type) -> Type:
+  Result<&1, &1, (U32 & String), A>
+
+def requirements_from_words(words: (U32 & U32) & ((U32 & U32) & U32)) -> MemoryRequirements:
+  (size, (alignment, bits)) = words
+  MemoryRequirements{Core.size_from_words(size), Core.size_from_words(alignment), bits}
+
+def requirements_result(result: VkResult<((U32 & U32) & ((U32 & U32) & U32))>) -> VkResult<MemoryRequirements>:
+  match result:
+    case Fail{error}:
+      Fail{error}
+    case Done{words}:
+      Done{requirements_from_words(words)}
+
+def Device.get_buffer_memory_requirements(device: Device, buffer: Buffer) -> IO(VkResult<MemoryRequirements>):
+  do IO<VkResult<MemoryRequirements>>:
+    result : VkResult<((U32 & U32) & ((U32 & U32) & U32))> <- Device.buffer_requirements_raw(device, buffer)
+    return requirements_result(result)
+
+def memory_types_from_words(words: List<(U32 & U32)>) -> List<Core.MemoryType>:
+  match words:
+    case Nil{}:
+      Nil{}
+    case Con{(flags, heap), rest}:
+      Core.MemoryType{flags, heap} <> memory_types_from_words(rest)
+
+def memory_types_result(result: VkResult<List<(U32 & U32)>>) -> VkResult<List<Core.MemoryType>>:
+  match result:
+    case Fail{error}:
+      Fail{error}
+    case Done{words}:
+      Done{memory_types_from_words(words)}
+
+def Instance.get_physical_device_memory_properties(instance: Instance, physical: PhysicalDevice) -> IO(VkResult<List<Core.MemoryType>>>):
+  do IO<VkResult<List<Core.MemoryType>>>:
+    result : VkResult<List<(U32 & U32)>> <- Instance.memory_types_raw(instance, physical)
+    return memory_types_result(result)
+
+def Entry.finish(-A: Type, result: VkResult<A>, cleanup: VkResult<Unit>) -> VkResult<A>:
+  match result cleanup:
+    case Fail{error} _:
+      Fail{error}
+    case Done{value} Done{unit}:
+      Done{value}
+    case Done{value} Fail{error}:
+      Fail{error}
+
+def Entry.run_loaded(-A: Type, body: Entry -> IO(VkResult<A>), loaded: VkResult<Entry>) -> IO(VkResult<A>):
+  match loaded:
+    case Fail{error}:
+      IO.pure(VkResult<A>, Fail{error})
+    case Done{+entry}:
+      do IO<VkResult<A>>:
+        result : VkResult<A> <- body(entry)
+        cleanup : VkResult<Unit> <- Entry.close(entry)
+        return Entry.finish(A, result, cleanup)
+
+def Entry.with(-A: Type, body: Entry -> IO(VkResult<A>)) -> IO(VkResult<A>):
+  do IO<VkResult<A>>:
+    loaded : VkResult<Entry> <- Entry.load()
+    Entry.run_loaded(A, body, loaded)
+
