text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat > /tmp/bend-vulkan-m2/framing.md <<'EOF'
# Milestone 2 framing and verification contract

Workspace /home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan-milestone1, branch feat/offscreen-images, stacked locally on completed milestone 1 at 1769c3107ffdd1bb27be9dc39478046c62d7d32b. No remote or configured author exists. Local commits use Codex <codex@localhost> via per-command git configuration. The pinned bend-collections submodule is initialized. Bend 2.0.37 guide was rerun. tools/verify.py --sanitize passed as a fresh baseline; log is baseline-verification.log beside this file.

## Definition of done

Every docs/roadmap.md milestone-2 item is implemented and exercised: explicit image creation/destruction and memory requirements/binding; views, layouts, aspects and ranges; Vulkan 1.0 render passes/framebuffers with color and depth attachments; explicit image clear and buffer-image copy/readback commands; dependency-safe cleanup; and documented dimensions, stride, channel order and color encoding. A real native program selects supported formats, clears a known optimal-tiled color target, transitions it, copies it to a host-readable buffer, observes fence completion, and verifies every pixel. Repeat with reused command resources and bounded live rows. Check wrong-device, unsupported-format, stale-handle, range, render-scope, pending protection, reset and failure cleanup. No graphics pipelines, shaders, draw/meshing or presentation in this milestone.

A nonuniform buffer upload/subrectangle with padded rows and nonzero offsets should prove copy addressing and orientation, beyond uniform-color clear. Color+depth render-pass begin/end and clears must execute on the GPU, not merely construct handles. Choose an exact representable clear expectation. Prefer D32_SFLOAT depth readback evidence if supported, without asserting unsupported hardware features. Separate actual-driver evidence from injected error paths. Keep existing milestone-1 tests green, preserve returned array ownership, exact VkResult bits and bend-collections U64.

## Scope and rigor

Roughly four new handle kinds (Image, ImageView, RenderPass, Framebuffer), about eighteen new effects, new configuration/region/value types, dispatch/constants, and coupled native/API/generator/tests/docs. Architecture determines the supported image profile before code. Use four or five coherent verified units, not parallel writers on shared source. Rigor is high because FFI layouts, dependent native lifetimes, render scopes and image synchronization can fail despite successful compilation or a single readback.

The designed workflow is baseline and reference grounding, parallel architecture candidates plus cross-judge, one implementation owner in ordered checked commits, real GPU and controlled boundary checks, no-comments before source review, independent parent verification, and a reviewed decision trail. PR creation is attempted only if a remote exists. All configured roles use codex/gpt-6.1-sol by the user's override.

## Voltra reference

User requested https://github.com/amage-si/voltra beforehand. Root cloned /tmp/bend-vulkan-m2/voltra at 8900b07e14b80d3528a3b38cb5b376774441d240 and read its AGENTS/license, offscreen target, readback conversion, command encoding/barrier policy, and bridge entry points. Dedicated read-only exploration is running before architecture. Voltra targets Vulkan 1.3 and UI-specific 2D rendering, with dynamic rendering and 0xRRGGBBAA logical colors. Our wrapper remains an explicit Vulkan 1.0 subset with returnable errors and upstream U64. Do not transplant Voltra's Vulkan declarations, 1.3 assumptions, fail-fast policy, U32 byte sizes or color swizzles. If adapting implementation rather than ideas, preserve required license notices and pinned provenance. Prefer fresh code against Khronos structs and our existing ABI.

## Questions architecture must settle

- Whole image shape, format/aspect metadata, supported mip/layer/sample/type profile, and what is explicitly rejected. Do not claim full Vulkan image support from a narrow verifier. Compare two structurally different ownership/layout approaches.
- Image views and framebuffer/render-pass dependencies must keep their images/allocations alive. Current generic BvUse edges can extend to native object dependencies; current host-busy lookup only follows one buffer binding and is insufficient for framebuffer -> view -> image -> memory. Keep one authoritative dependency model.
- Recording is not execution. Either keep image layouts an explicit caller responsibility or design a command-local transition ledger with safe submit/completion/reset/failure semantics. Never mutate a global actual-layout cache while merely recording. Avoid duplicate mutable pending truth.
- Command render scope needs explicit Outside/Inside state. Nested begin, end without begin, command end inside, and transfer/barrier/fill operations inside unsupported render scope must reject before void dispatch. Successful reset clears scope and refs; failed reset retains refs.
- Framebuffer attachment compatibility, same-device ownership, image-view ranges, render-area bounds, clear-value type/count, and color/depth usage and formats require boundary checks. Reference and marshaling allocations must succeed before void command calls.
- Query image-format configurations using vkGetPhysicalDeviceImageFormatProperties, not just generic format flags. Preserve exact FORMAT_NOT_SUPPORTED results. Check extent/mip/layer/sample/tiling/usage support before unsafe creation.
- Buffer-image addressing needs checked U64 multiplication/addition for offsets, row length/image height/layers and final byte span, format/aspect byte sizes, alignment, bounds, and memory alias policy. Explain image/buffer shared allocations and bufferImageGranularity; do not assume distinct handles imply distinct memory. Handle selected queue minImageTransferGranularity or explicitly scope image copy to queues where that restriction is satisfied. Depth copies need queue capability validation for the Vulkan 1.0 baseline.
- Barriers remain legacy 1.0, explicit stage/access/layout/range, IGNORED family indices. Decide whether to extend unified pipeline_barrier with images and migrate all callers in one wave, or explain another small coherent boundary. Preserve validated stage/access policy and no implicit CommandBuffer.end barrier.
- Probe emitted Bend layouts for all composite inputs, Maybe/list nesting and F32/clear-value unions. Use raw limb adapters for U64 outputs; never CID imported aliases. Packed uploads and readback continue to obey byte order and affine ownership contracts.

## Throughput checkpoint

Blocking first steps are Voltra/local grounding, a passing baseline and image/dependency/render-scope design. Independent readers and temp design artifacts parallelize; coupled implementation has one owner. Shared registry mutations stay on the IO event loop and each temp artifact has a separate owner. One actual code owner is the smallest safe decomposition because image resources, scopes, commands, generated ABI, tests and cleanup change together.

## Evidence limits

This CachyOS machine still lacks vulkan-validation-layers. Record validation/synchronization validation as unavailable unless environment changes. Do not count zero driver messages as Khronos validation. Hardware loss must not be provoked; use emitted-test-only dispatch substitution as in milestone 1. ASan leak detection is disabled for driver globals; wrapper cleanup needs explicit zero-row and dependency evidence. No speedup claim or benchmark is needed.

bash /home/aivv/.agents/skills/show-me-your-work/scripts/log.sh /tmp/bend-vulkan-m2/decisions.tsv frame 'Require real color/depth targets and every-pixel readback before marking milestone complete' 'A uniform image or constructor-only pass cannot establish copy addressing, render scopes or nested resource lifetime safety' /tmp/bend-vulkan-m2/framing.md 'scope and high-rigor gates recorded before code'",max_output_tokens:1000}));

Registry order can free allocations before associated images/buffers; replacements use different orders. `native/voltra.c:584–599,1198–1207`; `gpu.bend:108,138,575–583,623,685`.

- What runtime evidence will establish general F32/depth-clear ABI behavior? Voltra cannot answer this.

## Components Found

Voltra provides evidence for image allocation, staging transfers, and pixel verification. Its rendering layer differs substantially from milestone 2.

- `Texture` groups image, allocation, view, and dimensions. `Target` distinguishes swapchain targets from an owned offscreen image. Offscreen `Canvas` aliases that image without owning another allocation. `gpu.bend:117–178,301–312`.
- `Gpu` combines these resources with two frame contexts, upload commands, staging/readback buffers, and a destruction registry. `gpu.bend:422–435`.
- `commands.bend` defines command values, encoding, structural validation, and synchronization policy. `native.bend` declares effects. `native/voltra.c` translates words into Vulkan structures and calls.

## Flow

1. **Open.** `open_offscreen` creates an instance, enumerates GPUs, chooses a Vulkan 1.3 device, selects a graphics queue, and queries memory types. It creates the target and the complete quad-rendering infrastructure, including shaders, descriptors, two frame contexts, and an uploaded white texel. This is substantially more than an image constructor. `gpu.bend:1340–1397,1436–1463`.

2. **Create, allocate, bind, view.** `offscreen` requests optimal-tiled `B8G8R8A8_UNORM` with color-attachment and transfer-source usage. Native `vk_image` fixes 2D extent, depth 1, one mip, one layer, one sample, exclusive sharing, and initial `UNDEFINED` layout. It returns `[slot, requiredSize, alignment, memoryTypeBits]`. Bend selects device-local memory, allocates the required size, binds at offset zero, and creates an identity-swizzled view. Views expose an aspect argument but fix the subresource to one mip/layer. `gpu.bend:129–146,306–312`; `native/voltra.c:1144–1161,1197–1208,1296–1309`.

3. **Clear and render.** `C.frame` transitions `UNDEFINED` to color-attachment layout, begins dynamic rendering with `LOAD_OP_CLEAR`, draws, ends rendering, and transitions to transfer-source layout. The final barrier connects color-output writes to transfer reads. Native image barriers use legacy `vkCmdPipelineBarrier`, ignored queue-family indices, and a hardcoded color aspect/single subresource. `commands.bend:115–136,194–211`; `native/voltra.c:1642–1663`.

4. **Upload.** `upload` waits for device idle, replaces the sampled texture when dimensions change, ensures mapped host-visible coherent staging storage, copies array words into it, and records buffer-to-image transfer. The image transitions through `UNDEFINED`, transfer-destination, and shader-read layouts. Rectangle updates preserve other texels through shader-read/transfer-destination transitions. Native copy regions use zero row-length/image-height fields for tightly packed rows. `gpu.bend:727–748,784–811`; `commands.bend:158–183`; `native/voltra.c:1700–1717`.

5. **Read.** `read` accepts offscreen targets only. It waits idle, ensures a coherent mapped transfer-destination buffer, copies the target image into that buffer, records transfer-write to host-read synchronization, submits, and waits on a fence. Native `vk_read` then copies mapped words into a Bend array. Bend converts BGRA storage to `0xRRGGBBAA`. The logical layout is top-left, row-major, `width × height`, with `width × 4` bytes per row and no vertical flip. Array capacity can exceed the logical pixel count. `gpu.bend:1236–1305`; `commands.bend:167–172`; `native/voltra.c:1718–1729`; `shaders/prim.vert:25–28`.

6. **Close and verify.** `close` waits idle, destroys registry entries, and reports live slots and debug messages. GPU tests draw/read/compare every logical pixel against Bend expectations, covering texture channels/alpha, clipping, shapes, retained paints, same-frame uploads, stored quads, and resize. Teardown results are printed rather than asserted. `gpu.bend:1310–1331`; `gpu_tests.bend:75–87,233–289,365–442`.

## Non-Obvious Things

- **F32 is avoided at the Bend boundary.** Clear colors arrive as packed RGBA8; C divides channels by `255.0f`. Viewport dimensions likewise become C floats. This establishes neither general Bend F32 marshalling nor depth-clear support. `native/voltra.c:1655–1666`.

1. Creation loads dispatch at the relevant level. Native-resource creation followed by registry failure destroys the new native object. Physical-device enumeration interns existing handles within their instance. 2. Buffer binding checks common device ownership, previous binding, requirement size, offset alignment, and memory-type bits. Only successful `BindBufferMemory` assigns `bound` and `offset`. Freeing memory scans every row’s `bound` pointer. [native.c:755](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan-milestone1/src/native.c:755), [native.c:767](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan-milestone1/src/native.c:767).

## Components Found

Voltra provides evidence for image allocation, staging transfers, and pixel verification. Its rendering layer differs substantially from milestone 2.

- `Texture` groups image, allocation, view, and dimensions. `Target` distinguishes swapchain targets from an owned offscreen image. Offscreen `Canvas` aliases that image without owning another allocation. `gpu.bend:117–178,301–312`.
- `Gpu` combines these resources with two frame contexts, upload commands, staging/readback buffers, and a destruction registry. `gpu.bend:422–435`.
- `commands.bend` defines command values, encoding, structural validation, and synchronization policy. `native.bend` declares effects. `native/voltra.c` translates words into Vulkan structures and calls.

## Flow

1. **Open.** `open_offscreen` creates an instance, enumerates GPUs, chooses a Vulkan 1.3 device, selects a graphics queue, and queries memory types. It creates the target and the complete quad-rendering infrastructure, including shaders, descriptors, two frame contexts, and an uploaded white texel. This is substantially more than an image constructor. `gpu.bend:1340–1397,1436–1463`.

2. **Create, allocate, bind, view.** `offscreen` requests optimal-tiled `B8G8R8A8_UNORM` with color-attachment and transfer-source usage. Native `vk_image` fixes 2D extent, depth 1, one mip, one layer, one sample, exclusive sharing, and initial `UNDEFINED` layout. It returns `[slot, requiredSize, alignment, memoryTypeBits]`. Bend selects device-local memory, allocates the required size, binds at offset zero, and creates an identity-swizzled view. Views expose an aspect argument but fix the subresource to one mip/layer. `gpu.bend:129–146,306–312`; `native/voltra.c:1144–1161,1197–1208,1296–1309`.

3. **Clear and render.** `C.frame` transitions `UNDEFINED` to color-attachment layout, begins dynamic rendering with `LOAD_OP_CLEAR`, draws, ends rendering, and transitions to transfer-source layout. The final barrier connects color-output writes to transfer reads. Native image barriers use legacy `vkCmdPipelineBarrier`, ignored queue-family indices, and a hardcoded color aspect/single subresource. `commands.bend:115–136,194–211`; `native/voltra.c:1642–1663`.

4. **Upload.** `upload` waits for device idle, replaces the sampled texture when dimensions change, ensures mapped host-visible coherent staging storage, copies array words into it, and records buffer-to-image transfer. The image transitions through `UNDEFINED`, transfer-destination, and shader-read layouts. Rectangle updates preserve other texels through shader-read/transfer-destination transitions. Native copy regions use zero row-length/image-height fields for tightly packed rows. `gpu.bend:727–748,784–811`; `commands.bend:158–183`; `native/voltra.c:1700–1717`.

5. **Read.** `read` accepts offscreen targets only. It waits idle, ensures a coherent mapped transfer-destination buffer, copies the target image into that buffer, records transfer-write to host-read synchronization, submits, and waits on a fence. Native `vk_read` then copies mapped words into a Bend array. Bend converts BGRA storage to `0xRRGGBBAA`. The logical layout is top-left, row-major, `width × height`, with `width × 4` bytes per row and no vertical flip. Array capacity can exceed the logical pixel count. `gpu.bend:1236–1305`; `commands.bend:167–172`; `native/voltra.c:1718–1729`; `shaders/prim.vert:25–28`.

6. **Close and verify.** `close` waits idle, destroys registry entries, and reports live slots and debug messages. GPU tests draw/read/compare every logical pixel against Bend expectations, covering texture channels/alpha, clipping, shapes, retained paints, same-frame uploads, stored quads, and resize. Teardown results are printed rather than asserted. `gpu.bend:1310–1331`; `gpu_tests.bend:75–87,233–289,365–442`.

## Boundaries

- Useful reference mechanisms include explicit create/requirements/allocate/bind/view sequencing, staging readback, explicit barriers, logical array lengths, independent pixel expectations, and official-header ABI comparisons.
- Milestone 2 requires Vulkan 1.0 render passes/framebuffers and color/depth attachments. Voltra enables dynamic rendering, supplies one color attachment, and has no depth implementation. Its offscreen path still enables Xlib instance extensions and the swapchain device extension. `native/voltra.c:711–715,865–891,1548–1550,1659–1660`.
- Voltra assumes coherent host memory and uses U32 sizes/offsets, including truncating native memory requirements. These differ from the target’s U64, noncoherent-memory, ownership, recorded-reference, and failure-cleanup requirements. `gpu.bend:98–108`; `native/voltra.c:1159–1160`; roadmap:208–219.
- Copying requires provenance and the selected license’s notices. Voltra offers MIT or Apache-2.0. MIT identifies AMAGE copyright and requires retaining its notice. No implementation was copied.

## Non-Obvious Things

- **F32 is avoided at the Bend boundary.** Clear colors arrive as packed RGBA8; C divides channels by `255.0f`. Viewport dimensions likewise become C floats. This establishes neither general Bend F32 marshalling nor depth-clear support. `native/voltra.c:1655–1666`.
- **Arrays return on failure too.** Effects directly access runtime blocks through `blk_cls`/`blk_loc`, then return the original array alongside `Result`. `settle` drops it; readback retains and converts it. Transfers still perform `memcpy`. JS failure paths preserve the array too. `native/voltra.c:658–662,1242–1285`; `gpu.bend:58–61,1251–1256`; `native/voltra.js:13–14,37–44`.
- **Pixel packing is deliberate.** Little-endian packed upload words become A,B,G,R bytes; sampled-image views reverse components. Readback separately converts BGRA. UNORM storage carries encoded-sRGB values without gamma conversion. `gpu.bend:120–127,1236–1239`; `policy.bend:230–235`.
- **ABI coverage has limits.** The checker compiles two layout probes. `VkClearValue` receives only a size comparison; the bridge substitutes a simplified float/int/uint union. Function signatures, Bend runtime blocks, and F32 semantics are outside that check. `native/abi_check.py:24–29,57–105`; `native/voltra.c:62–63`.
- **README safety claims need qualification.** Slots have no generations, can be reused, and binding/view checks do not compare owning devices. `once` ignores timeout status. Registry order can free allocations before associated images/buffers; replacements use different orders. `native/voltra.c:584–599,1198–1207`; `gpu.bend:108,138,575–583,623,685`.
- README’s pixel results and negative-control result are historical claims. The committed tests support the comparison mechanism but do not establish those results here. Validation-layer coverage is explicitly pending. `README.md:77–113,250–253`.

## Open Questions

- Which target acceptance checks will cover unsupported formats, wrong-device operands, failed creation cleanup, and resource destruction while commands reference images?
- How should read-before-first-render and zero-sized offscreen targets behave? Voltra’s read path does not establish valid rendered contents.
- What runtime evidence will establish general F32/depth-clear ABI behavior? Voltra cannot answer this.

1. **Why this shape exists.** [docs/design.md](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/docs/design.md:3) explains that Bend permits fabricated ordinary constructors and cannot extend opaque host handles. C therefore owns pointers and dispatch; Bend exposes distinct `Data` handles containing monotonic U32 keys. Affine wrappers alone would neither ensure native destruction nor avoid threading owners through results. Temporary copy-based mapping avoids exposed pointer/cache lifetimes. Registry changes run exclusively on the IO event loop; pure preparation can parallelize.

2. **Normal recording/submission.** In [src/native.c](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/src/native.c:635), `bv_begin_command_buffer` accepts only state `0`, requests `ONE_TIME_SUBMIT`, and enters recording `1`. `bv_cmd_fill_buffer` checks ownership, binding, transfer-destination usage, bounds, and four-byte alignment, then records a `BvUse` before calling Vulkan. `bv_end_command_buffer` currently inserts transfer-write→host-read synchronization and enters executable `2`. `bv_submit_and_wait` marks command `3` and device `1` before `QueueSubmit`, then calls `QueueWaitIdle`. Success clears device state; command state remains `3`.

3. **Failure behavior.** Begin/end Vulkan failures set command state `4`; rejected fill arguments leave recording intact. [bv_submit_and_wait](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/src/native.c:680) conservatively retains device state after submit/wait errors other than device loss. Buffer/pool destruction, memory freeing, host copies, and further submissions then reject operations. `bv_device_wait_idle` clears that state on success or device loss. Thus device `state` presently means unresolved completion after failure, rather than a complete asynchronous submission model. A failed submission cannot automatically rely on its fence eventually signaling.

4. **References and teardown.** [BvRow/BvUse and destruction helpers](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/src/native.c:17) encode `entry→instance→device→pool→command` ownership, plus command→buffer references and buffer→allocation bindings. References survive successful submission and completion; `bv_remove` releases them only when removing the command, currently through pool destruction. Completion therefore does not itself make buffers destroyable. [Entry.with/Entry.finish](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/Vulkan.bend:226) run cleanup after returned success/failure and preserve the callback error, appending cleanup errors. [bv_entry_close](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/src/native.c:221) waits, destroys pools/references, buffers, allocations, devices, instances, then unloads. Non-device-loss wait failure leaves the remaining tree live for retry.

5. **Asynchronous/reset constraints.** [Milestone 1](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/docs/roadmap.md:43) specifies one queue, one submission in flight, legacy Vulkan 1.0 synchronization, distinct recording/executable/pending/completed/invalid states, and `submit_and_wait` built over general submission. Pending commands, pools, fences, referenced buffers, and bound allocations need protection; mapped access must also respect pending GPU use. Completion observed through fence status/wait or device idle must reconcile the same pending associations. Successful reset releases recorded references; unsuccessful reset must retain them. [Pool creation](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/src/native.c:597) currently supplies no flags, so individual command-buffer reset requires enabling the relevant pool capability. Completed one-time commands require reset/re-recording before reuse; completion must not restore executable status. Despite “reusable command recording” in design prose, current behavior is one-shot.

6. **Barrier/copy boundary.** `CommandBuffer.end` must stop selecting synchronization for callers. [The fill example](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/examples/buffer_roundtrip.bend:47) currently depends on its hidden host-read barrier. Copies need source and destination ownership, binding, usage, range, and overlap validation, plus references to both buffers. Barrier-recorded buffer handles need references too. Allocate reference bookkeeping before issuing void Vulkan recording commands. [bv_create_device](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/src/native.c:380) selects queue zero from one family; buffers use exclusive sharing. Barrier family indices must express that intent explicitly. Zero-initialized family indices imply family zero, not “ignored.” Stage/access masks must suit the selected family; the existing pool check accepts graphics, compute, or transfer capability.

7. **Packed upload opportunity and ownership.** [bv_write_memory](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/src/native.c:540) currently consumes byte-valued `List<U32>`, grows a temporary byte buffer, maps the entire allocation, copies a checked subrange, flushes noncoherent memory, and unmaps. Packed words can avoid list traversal and conversion storage. Explicit byte length must be bounded by array capacity and allocation range, including partial final words and byte-order policy. Every outcome must explicitly return the affine array or consume/release it. Never retain a Bend heap pointer after relinquishing ownership. Existing generated runtime [block helpers](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/build/native-tests.c:1311) distinguish packed `TAG_BUF` U32 storage from `TAG_ARR` Terms; shared blocks use `blk_loc`. Source-level `ALeaf/ANode` syntax is insufficient ABI evidence. Probe emitted upload signatures before assuming layout.

8. **U64 and result traps.** [FFI rationale](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/docs/design.md:31) documents flattened `BufferCreateInfo` limbs and tuple-based U64 outputs. Preserve upstream `W.U64` for offsets, sizes, heap capacities, and fence timeouts; use subtraction-based range checks and wide arithmetic for array byte capacity. [VkResult/Action](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/Vulkan.bend:41) preserve exact result bits but short-circuit `Fail`. Fence `VK_NOT_READY` and `VK_TIMEOUT` must be ordinary returned statuses, without clearing pending work.

9. **Discovery, generation, evidence.** Current [physical/memory queries](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/src/native.c:339) expose basic identity and memory-type flags/heap indices, omitting limits, heap sizes, formats, and layer/extension enumeration. New queries need correct dispatch ownership, U64 adapters, and bounded count/retry handling. [bindings.json](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/tools/bindings.json:1) drives declarations, registrations, and JS rejection through [generate.py](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/tools/generate.py:45); C marshalling/dispatch remain manual. [tests/native.bend](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan/tests/native.bend:35) covers invalid states, recorded references, rejected resubmission, stale handles, U64 boundaries, and success/failure scope cleanup. Milestone 1 is complete on `feat/general-transfers`, at `1769c31`. Five ordered local commits are verified, and the worktree is clean. No PR was created because there is no remote.

The wrapper now provides explicit barriers, packed uploads that return array ownership, alias-checked buffer copies, fences, command reset, and capability queries. See the [API reference](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan-milestone1/docs/api.md).

| Choice | Tradeoff |
| --- | --- |
| Command-owned completion state | Model the Domain keeps one authoritative submission association. |
| Reset and re-record for reuse | Laziness Protocol keeps the initial API small. |
| One queue and one pending submission | Keeps lifetime checks bounded for this milestone. |

Boundary Discipline keeps validation at the native boundary. Build the Lever and Prove It Works produced rerunnable GPU and failure checks. Sequence Work into Verifiable Units shaped the commit order.

The throughput checkpoint used grounding and design as gates, isolated parallel designs, one owner for coupled implementation files, and parallel read-only verification. The IO loop remains the sole registry writer, following Separate Before Serializing Shared State.

Independent verification passed:

- 32 changing GPU upload/copy/readback cycles with stable resource counts.
- Ownership, pending-state, cleanup, and injected failure checks.
- ASan/UBSan, generator freshness, and `bend PROOF.bend --verdict`.

No architecture decisions remain open. [Milestone 2, offscreen images, is next](/home/aivv/Документы/projects/bend-vulkan-milestone1/docs/roadmap.md:75).

L191: # Synchronization Validation
L192: 
L193: Synchronization Validation (SyncVal) is part of the `VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation` layer. It identifies resource access conflicts caused by missing or incorrect synchronization between commands that read or write the same regions of memory.
L194: 
L195: We recommend running Synchronization Validation regularly during development, after resolving errors reported by core validation.
L196: 
L197: Report problems or request additional checks by creating a cite63†GitHub issue .
L198: ## Enabling Synchronization Validation
L199: 
L200: Enable the `VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation` layer and turn on its `validate_sync` cite72†layer setting .
L201: 
L202: Three common ways to enable Synchronization Validation are:
L203: 
L204:   1. Use cite73†Vulkan Configurator (vkconfig)†www.lunarg.com and select the Synchronization Only preset.
L205: 
L206: > NOTE - This preset disables other validation checks to reduce overhead.
L207:   2. Use `VK_EXT_layer_settings`
L208: 
L209:     // Will turn on as an additional setting with core validation
L210:     const VkBool32 enable_sync = VK_TRUE;
L211:     const VkLayerSettingEXT layer_setting = {"VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation", "validate_sync", VK_LAYER_SETTING_TYPE_BOOL32_EXT, 1, &enable_sync};
L212:     VkLayerSettingsCreateInfoEXT layer_settings_create_info = {VK_STRUCTURE_TYPE_LAYER_SETTINGS_CREATE_INFO_EXT, nullptr, 1, &layer_setting};
L213: 
L214:     VkInstanceCreateInfo instance_ci = GetYourCreateInfo();
L215:     instance_ci.pNext = &layer_settings_create_info;
L216:   3. Set as an environment variable (will turn on as an additional setting with core validation)
L217: 
L218:     # Windows
L219:     set VK_VALIDATION_VALIDATE_SYNC=1
L220: 
L221:     # Linux
L222:     export VK_VALIDATION_VALIDATE_SYNC=1
L223: 
L224:     # Android
L225:     adb shell setprop debug.vulkan.khronos_validation.validate_sync 1
L226: 
L227: There are additional cite74†SyncVal settings†vulkan.lunarg.com that use the `syncval_` prefix.
L228: ### When Errors Are Reported
L229: 
L230: Synchronization Validation runs its full set of checks when command buffers are submitted with `vkQueueSubmit` or `vkQueueSubmit2`. Every supported hazard is detected at this point.
L231: 
L232: Record-time reporting, enabled by default, runs a subset of these checks earlier, during command buffer recording. Errors it finds are reported at the `vkCmd*` call that causes the hazard, so a debugger can stop while the application is recording that command.
L233: Record-time reporting adds CPU overhead. If you do not need errors at record time, disable it with the `syncval_record_time_validation` setting or by turning off `Record-time reporting` in Vulkan Configurator. Validation coverage is unchanged, all errors are reported at submission, and validation runs faster.
L234: ## Synchronization Validation Messages
L235: 
L236: A synchronization validation error message describes a race condition by identifying two memory accesses that caused the hazard and the state of applied synchronization.
L237: 
L238: Example of an error reported during `vkCmdExecuteCommands` with record-time reporting enabled:
L239: > vkCmdExecuteCommands(): WRITE_AFTER_READ hazard detected. vkCmdCopyImage (from the secondary VkCommandBuffer 0x1fb2f224d40) writes to VkImage 0xf56c9b0000000004, which was previously read by another vkCmdCopyImage command (from the primary VkCommandBuffer 0x1fb245f4200).
L240: >
L241: > No sufficient synchronization is present to ensure that a write (VK_ACCESS_2_TRANSFER_WRITE_BIT) at VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_2_COPY_BIT does not conflict with a prior read (VK_ACCESS_2_TRANSFER_READ_BIT) at the same stage.
L242: >
L243: > Vulkan insight: an execution dependency is sufficient to prevent this hazard.
L244: The error message usually includes the following:
L245:   * The Vulkan API function at which the error was reported. For errors reported during submission, this is the queue submission call, while the message identifies the recorded commands involved in the hazard.
L246:   * A brief description of the type of race condition (e.g., WRITE_AFTER_WRITE)
L247:   * The commands that performed memory accesses and the resource involved (e.g., vkCmdCopyBuffer and vkCmdDispatch accessing the same VkBuffer)
L248:   * Synchronization details: pipeline stages, access types, and applied synchronization
L249:   * In some cases, a "Vulkan insight" section at the end of the error message may provide additional information related to the current error
L250: Unlike core validation error messages, where each message is identified by a VUID, synchronization validation primarily detects a single type of error: a race condition between two memory accesses. There are limitless ways to produce a race condition (combinations of command pairs and different synchronization methods), which is why race condition scenarios are not identified by VUIDs.
L251: To suppress or filter synchronization validation error messages, one can use the optional `Extra properties` section. Extra properties contain key-value pairs that help identify the error message and are presented in a more structured format compared to the main error message, making parsing easier.
L252: One of the benefits of parsing `Extra properties` rather than the main error message is that the former is more stable and changes less frequently. This creates a nice separation: on one side, we can take every opportunity to improve the error message wording while keeping the Extra properties values unchanged in most cases, so suppression and filtering logic does not need to be updated.
L253: 
L254: Example of error message with extra properties enabled:
L255: > vkQueueSubmit(): WRITE_AFTER_WRITE hazard detected. vkCmdEndRenderPass (from VkCommandBuffer submitted on the current VkQueue ) writes to resource, which was previously written by vkCmdClearColorImage (from VkCommandBuffer submitted on VkQueue ).
L256: >
L257: > The current synchronization allows VK_ACCESS_2_COLOR_ATTACHMENT_READ_BIT accesses at VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_2_COLOR_ATTACHMENT_OUTPUT_BIT, but to prevent this hazard, it must allow VK_ACCESS_2_COLOR_ATTACHMENT_WRITE_BIT accesses at VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_2_COLOR_ATTACHMENT_OUTPUT_BIT.
L258: 
L259:     `[Extra properties]
L260:     message_type = SubmitTimeError
L261:     hazard_type = WRITE_AFTER_WRITE
L262:     prior_access = VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_2_CLEAR_BIT(VK_ACCESS_2_TRANSFER_WRITE_BIT)
L263:     write_barriers = VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_2_COLOR_ATTACHMENT_OUTPUT_BIT(VK_ACCESS_2_COLOR_ATTACHMENT_READ_BIT)
L264:     command = vkCmdEndRenderPass
L265:     prior_command = vkCmdClearColorImage
L266:     command_buffer_index = 1
L267:     submit_index = 2
L268:     batch_index = 0
L269:     batch_tag = 5
L270:     `
L271: Extra properties can be enabled in Vulkan Configurator or by using the `syncval_message_extra_properties` validation layer setting.
L272: ## Synchronization Validation Functionality
L273: ### Overview
L274: 
L275: The pipelined and multi-threaded nature of Vulkan makes it particularly important for applications to correctly insert needed synchronization primitives, and for validation to diagnose unprotected memory access hazards. Synchronization Validation reports the presence of access hazards including information to identify the Vulkan operations which are in conflict. The reported hazards are:
L276: RAW  | Read-after-write  | Occurs when a subsequent operation uses the result of a previous operation without waiting for the result to be completed.
L277: WAR  | Write-after-read  | Occurs when a subsequent operation overwrites a memory location read by a previous operation before that operation is complete (requires only execution dependency).
L278: WAW  | Write-after-write  | Occurs when a subsequent operation writes to the same set of memory locations (in whole or in part) being written by a previous operation.
L279: WRW  | Write-racing-write  | Occurs when unsynchronized subpasses/queues perform writes to the same set of memory locations.
L280: RRW  | Read-racing-write  | Occurs when unsynchronized subpasses/queues perform read and write operations on the same set of memory locations.
L281: ### Current Features
L282:   * Hazard detection within and between command buffers, submissions, and queues.
L283:   * Pipeline barriers, event operations, and render pass dependencies, including synchronization2 commands from Vulkan 1.3 and `VK_KHR_synchronization2`.
L284:   * Image layout transition hazard and access tracking.
L285:   * Attachment load, store, and resolve operations in render passes and dynamic rendering.
L286:   * Secondary command buffers executed with `vkCmdExecuteCommands`.
L287:   * Semaphore and fence synchronization, and device and queue wait-idle operations.
L288: ### Known Limitations
L289:   * Does not support precise tracking of descriptors accessed by the shader (requires integration with GPU-AV). This includes both classic VkDescriptorSet and VK_EXT_descriptor_buffer APIs
L290:   * Hazards related to memory aliasing are not detected properly
L291:   * Indirectly accessed buffers (indirect data/indexed vertex data) are not validated
L292:   * Host set event not supported
L293:   * No dedicated support for sparse resources
L294:   * Host memory accesses are not tracked. Corresponding race conditions are not reported
L295:   * Does not include component granularity access tracking, or correctly support swizzling
L296: ## Synchronization blogs/articles
L297: 
L298: Synchronization Examples cite75†https://github.com/KhronosGroup/Vulkan-Docs/wiki/Synchronization-Examples L299: 
L300: Keeping your GPU fed without getting bitten cite76†https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oF7vOTTaAh4†www.youtube.com L301:

The validation-layer package isn’t installed on your CachyOS system. `pacman -Q vulkan-validation-layers` reports it missing, and Vulkan’s layer list contains no `VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation`.

Synchronization validation is part of that same layer, so both were unavailable. [Khronos documentation](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/Vulkan-ValidationLayers/blob/main/docs/syncval_usage.md).

Install it, then rerun verification:

```sh
sudo pacman -S vulkan-validation-layers
VK_VALIDATION_VALIDATE_SYNC=1 python3 tools/verify.py --sanitize
```

The verifier detects the installed layer and runs the GPU checks with validation enabled.

Delegate code-writing with `delegate_task` (`mode: "async"`, a self-contained brief drained with `task_status`) using the `feature, refactoring` role from `p3-models.md`, resolved through `orchestrator_capabilities`, with a specific scope (file paths, named data shape and its organizing structure per **principle-model-the-domain**, a state machine over scattered booleans, a table/registry over branching, a typed model over repeated shape assumptions, chosen before the delegate writes logic, and success criteria). When the implementation admits multiple valid shapes (error handling, abstraction layer, test structure), delegate via the **arena** skill instead so the runners surface the alternatives and the cross-judge guards the pick. 5. Verify on the matching surface. "Inconclusive" or wrong-surface is not a pass. Flag it.
6. Rebase into small, ordered commits. Stack follow-ups.
   Use the **sequence-verifiable-units** principle skill, building, verifying, and committing each small unit before the next.
7. If the design is contested, `interrogate` before shipping.

Code-coupled work (one feature, one migration) goes to a single owner with the checkpoint inline. That owner fans out internally after the blocking phase. name: figure-it-out
description: "Design an auditable playbook when no narrower one fits: a large migration, an ambitious multi-part change, or work a human reviews after stepping away. Scales rigor to the task, runs a hypothesis loop, and logs decisions via show-me-your-work. Use for /figure-it-out, 'figure it out', a large migration, or when no narrower playbook applies."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Figure it out

When the task matches no playbook, design one. The deliverable before any code is the workflow itself: a sequence of phases that scales rigor to the task, runs the scientific method, and leaves a decision trail a human can audit after stepping away.

## Start

Open a todolist whose first item is to read the Principles section of the **p3-mode** skill. Then add the phases below as todos.

## Phase A: Frame

Ground first, then commit. Don't start the run until you can state:

- The definition of done as a falsifiable predicate (the **prove-it-works** principle skill).
- Scope, quantified: rough units and effort, plus the blockers grounding surfaced.
- The rigor level, biased high. One-way doors and high blast radius get more. Reversible low-stakes steps get less. Rigor is gates and artifacts, not "try harder".

Present the framing and tradeoffs before committing to a long run. Reversible work proceeds (the **never-block-on-the-human** principle skill), but a multi-hour run earns one checkpoint.

## Phase B: Design the workflow

Decompose into atomic, independently-landable units. Sequence riskiest-unknown-first. Scaffold and verification come before features (the **foundational-thinking** principle skill).

- Build the verification harness before the work, with the baseline captured from the pre-change state, so the check reads as "old value vs new value".
- For one-way-door design decisions, run the **architect** skill (it runs **arena**). Skip it for mechanical work whose shape is already concrete. A second arena over a settled design is over-engineering (the **laziness-protocol** principle skill).
- Decide what fans out. Parallelize only across seams, and give each writer its own worktree via `t3_thread_launch` with a `workspaceStrategy`, one writer per worktree (the **separate-before-serializing-shared-state** principle skill). Don't over-fan.
- Every `delegate_task` brief stands alone: the child gets only the brief, never your context. Read-only workers get a brief that says read-only, inspect only, no writes. Resolve models from named roles in `p3-models.md` via `orchestrator_capabilities`; never hardcode a slug.
- Write the designed phase list down. That list is what the human reviews.

Then execute the design. Add its steps to the todolist as concrete items, after the Phase C entry and before Phase D. Run each under the Phase C loop discipline, and weave the Phase D log through them, a row as each step lands, rather than saving the whole trail for the end.

## Phase C: Run the loop

Each unit is an experiment. State the hypothesis, make the smallest change, measure against the predicate on the real artifact, keep it if it advanced, revert it if it didn't.
Apply the **sequence-verifiable-units** principle skill, verifying each unit before starting the next instead of batching checks at the end.

- Verify by inspecting the artifact, never a self-report. When something passes too easily, suspect the observation method before the system.
- Pair delegated work with a judge. If a worker games the gate, reset and harden the contract. If the gate itself is wrong, fix the gate in its own change rather than routing around it.
- Drain background work with `task_status`. For a PR in flight, arm `watch_pull_request`, end the turn, and triage on wake; use `schedule_task` for recurring checks.
- A verdict is VERIFIED, NOT VERIFIED, or INCONCLUSIVE. Inconclusive is not a pass. Don't hide a negative.

## Phase D: Keep the audit trail

Log the run via the **show-me-your-work** skill. figure-it-out's work is usually ambitious enough to commit the trail so the reviewer can read it in the PR. The trail plus the diff is what lets the human come back and trust the work.

## Phase E: Verify and hand back

Check the whole against the Phase A predicate on the real product, not just the harness. Encode any recurring correction as a gate, a lint rule, a check, or a script (the **encode-lessons-in-structure** principle skill).

**Reply:** the playbook you designed, the rigor level and why, the decision-trail path, what's verified against the predicate, and what's still open.

name: how
description: "Use for \"how does X work\", code walkthroughs before changing something, and placement / ownership / layering questions (\"where should this live\", \"which package owns this\", \"is this the right layer\"). Explains subsystem architecture, runtime flow, onboarding mental models. Use why for motivation."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# How

Explore the codebase to answer "how does X work?" questions. Produce architectural explanations at the level of a senior engineer onboarding onto a subsystem, enough to build a working mental model, not so much that it reads like annotated source code.

Every spawn below is a `delegate_task` with a self-contained brief; the child gets only the brief, never this conversation. Each brief says it is read-only: inspect only, no writes, no git commands. Resolve each role's model from `p3-models.md` via `orchestrator_capabilities`. Never hardcode a slug. If the role line is missing, run `setup-p3` or use the parent's model.

## Step 1. Assess Complexity

If the scope is ambiguous, state your interpretation and explore. The user can redirect.

- **Simple** (a single module, a small utility, a narrow question such as "how does function X work"): no explorers. One explainer explores and explains in a single pass. Go to Step 2b.
- **Complex** (a subsystem spanning multiple files or services, a cross-cutting feature, a full architectural overview): spawn parallel explorers first, then hand off to the explainer. Go to Step 2a.

When in doubt, take the simple path.

## Step 2a. Explore (complex questions only)

Decompose the question into 2 to 4 exploration angles, each a distinct slice of the subsystem. Spawn all explorers in a single message, `mode: "async"`, model from the `how explorer` role.

Each explorer's brief is `references/explorer-prompt.md` with its angle filled in. Drain with `task_status`, then go to Step 3.

## Step 2b. Direct Explain (simple questions)

Spawn one `delegate_task` that explores and explains in one pass, model from the `how explainer` role.

Build its brief from `references/explainer-prompt.md` without the explorer-findings section. Go to Step 4.

## Step 3. Synthesize (complex questions only)

Once all explorers have returned, spawn one `delegate_task` to synthesize their findings into one explanation, model from the `how explainer` role.

Build its brief from `references/explainer-prompt.md` with every explorer's findings filled in.

## Step 4. Present

Present the explainer's output to the user. Light edits for clarity or context from the conversation are fine. Do not substantially rewrite it.

## Output Format

The explanation uses the sections defined in `references/explainer-prompt.md`, dropping any that do not apply: Overview, Key Concepts, How It Works, Where Things Live, Gotchas.

L230: # Voltra
L231: 
L232: GPU access and presentation for Bend 2, on Vulkan.
L233: Voltra is the GPU layer of the AMAGE UI ecosystem. It picks a Vulkan device, builds a swapchain for a window that cite112†Ankra owns (or an offscreen image), uploads textures and atlas regions, and draws instanced 2D quads: flat fills, images, coverage masks and antialiased rounded boxes and rings, each clipped. A retained canvas keeps the last picture, so a frame can redraw only the rectangles that changed and tell the compositor which ones they were. Then it presents, resizes and tears down cleanly.
L234: The library is written in Bend 2; the only native code is a thin, documented bridge of Vulkan calls exposed as Bend effects.
L235: Status: early Linux implementation, tested with Bend 2.0.36 on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Laptop GPU (driver 610.57.04, Vulkan 1.4.341) under Hyprland/XWayland. The first priority is a polished, measured experience on the development Linux machine. Compatibility layers will follow proven progress.
L236: The capture above is a frame rendered by cite113†Chromi on the CPU and presented by Voltra on the GPU in an Ankra window. It is identical, pixel for pixel, to Chromi's own output (all 604,800 pixels). Chromi's integrated demo (`examples/eco`) draws its frames through Voltra's 2D quads instead, redrawing only what changed; see its README.
L237: ## What works today
L238:   * Device selection: every Vulkan GPU is reported (type, vendor, device, API and driver versions, device-local memory, maximum image size), and the best Vulkan 1.3+ device that can present to the window is chosen.
L239:   * A presentation surface made from the native window Ankra hands over (Xlib `Display*` and window id). Voltra opens no window and reads no window events; window size changes come from Ankra's `Resized` events.
L240:   * A swapchain with explicit format, present mode (FIFO by default), image-count and composition choices, rebuilt on every real resize and on out-of-date or suboptimal presentation.
L241:   * A 2D primitive pipeline: one instanced draw of 16-word quads, five kinds (flat, nearest-texel image with tint, coverage mask, rounded box, ring), each with a clip box. Every coverage and color value is computed with integer arithmetic in the shader, so a CPU renderer following the same rules produces the same bytes. Straight-alpha source-over blending in encoded sRGB, as Chromi's CPU composition.
L242:   * A retained canvas per target (`paint`): the picture stays from one frame to the next, so a frame can redraw only some rectangles, each with its own instances and the scissor on it, before the canvas is copied into the acquired swapchain image; a whole paint clears it first (a first frame, a new size). The present then names the changed rectangles (`VK_KHR_incremental_present`, enabled when the device offers it). New atlas regions are copied inside the same frame, so the CPU never waits for the device.
L243: `draw` still draws whole frames straight into the image.
L244:   * Textures: whole-image uploads, blank textures with rectangle updates in one transfer (`update`), and an atlas allocator (`atlas.bend`, shelves; entries found by key in a persistent map, `keys.bend`).
L245:   * `keys.bend`: a persistent map from U32 keys to Data values (big-endian Patricia trie): lookups follow one branch per distinguishing bit and only borrow the map, `put`/`del` rebuild one path. The atlas and Chromi's demo text use it; any caller may.
L246:   * Offscreen targets and readback (`open_offscreen`, `read`), for pixel tests; `resize` makes an offscreen target again at a new size.
L247:   * Two frames in flight with per-frame fences, semaphores, command buffers and growable instance buffers.
L248:   * Ordered teardown of every native object, reporting leaked objects and the driver warnings and errors seen during the run.
L249: How it was verified on the development machine:
L250:   * 76 native checks (`tests.bend`) of the Bend-side logic: policies, command encoding and validation (patches, readback, memory barriers, image copies, and whole, partial and empty canvas paints), quad packing including clips and signed eighths, quadtree conversion, atlas packing, readback conversion and slot tracking. No display or GPU.
L251:   * 11 key map checks (`keys_tests.bend`): random puts, removals and lookups against a reference list (2 x 3000 operations), edge keys across the high bit, ascending order, persistence of older versions, and the depth of 450 atlas-style keys (13).
L252:   * 14 GPU checks (`gpu_tests.bend`, offscreen, no display): each quad kind drawn and read back, compared pixel by pixel with values computed in Bend by the shader's integer rules: flat quads with clips and translucency; every source byte at every alpha (texels); tinted texels; every coverage at every ink alpha; rounded boxes and rings; and the texel image over all 256 destination values (86 frames, 5,636,096 blended pixels). 0 pixels differ in every check on the RTX 3050.
L253: A deliberately wrong expectation was detected (2,850,560 differing pixels), so the comparison is not vacuous. The canvas: a whole paint, a partial paint of one changed box over the kept picture, a paint with nothing to redraw, and a partial paint that uploads a texture region and samples it in the same frame each equal the expected frame (0 differing pixels); an offscreen target made again at 128x96 holds no picture until a whole paint, which equals the frame.
L254:   * Visual: the quad example and the Chromi example captured from their own windows (`grim -T`) at their opening size and after resizes by the window manager (960x630, 500x760, 1280x480); the content follows each size. Chromi's demo and text grid, painted partially through Tab, activations and resizes, equal its previous full-redraw binaries in every capture.
L255:   * Present regions: an X client watching the window's damage (cite114†eco-bench `tools/damage.c`) saw each partial frame of Chromi's grid damage only its changed rectangles (3,400 to 4,900 pixels) instead of the whole 900x560 window (504,000 pixels) as without the extension, so XWayland hands the compositor about a hundredth of the window to recompose.
L256:   * Animation: `examples/motion.bend` (a rect sliding for 2 s through Ankra's `Loop.animate`) presented 241 frames per slide at a p50 interval of 8.43-8.47 ms and p99 9.55-9.62 ms on the 120 Hz panel, none dropped, then 0 frames and 0 main-thread wakeups; captures mid-slide and at rest (`grim -T`) show the rect moving and resting at x = 560.
L257:   * Pixel-exact: the GPU-presented Chromi frame equals the CPU reference written by `examples/reference.bend` (`magick compare -metric AE` 0).
L258:   * Teardown: every run ended with 0 native objects left and 0 driver warnings or errors. The Khronos validation layer is not installed on the development machine (package `vulkan-validation-layers`), so validation-layer coverage is still pending.
L259:   * ABI: `native/abi_check.py` compares 509 sizes and offsets of the bridge's Vulkan declarations (73 structs) with the official Khronos headers.
L260: ## Measurements
L261: 
L262: The same Chromi frame at 960x630, 600 frames per run, CPU time of the whole process from `/proc/self/stat` (10 ms ticks), three runs each, in a fixed-size Ankra window. Method and raw output: cite115†docs/bench.md .

L264: --- | --- | ---
L265: Official `Window` (CPU quadtree fill + `XPutImage`, runtime paced at 60 Hz)  | 16.6 ms  | 1.17–1.25 ms
L266: Voltra, unchanged content, FIFO  | 7.5–7.6 ms  | 0.30–0.32 ms
L267: Voltra, unchanged content, IMMEDIATE  | 0.17–0.19 ms  | 0.15–0.17 ms
L268: Voltra, new content every frame (raster in Bend + 2.4 MB upload), IMMEDIATE  | 1.1–1.2 ms  | 0.70–0.75 ms

With retained frames painted on the canvas, an activation in Chromi's 5000-label grid draws 21 quads and is presented 0.6 ms after the key (it drew about 20,000 quads in 32.9 ms); see the cite117†Eco vs GPUI benchmark .
L271: ## Quick start
L272: Requirements: the cite118†Bend 2 toolchain†bend-lang.com , Clang 14 or newer, X11 development headers/libraries, a Vulkan 1.3 driver with its loader (`libvulkan.so.1`), an X11 or XWayland display for windows, and cite112†Ankra cloned beside Voltra for the examples. Keep the capitalized directory names: Bend imports are case-sensitive. No Vulkan SDK or headers are needed to build.
L273: 
L274:     git clone https://github.com/amage-si/voltra.git Voltra
L275:     git clone https://github.com/amage-si/ankra.git Ankra
L276:     cd Voltra
L277:     export BEND_NO_TELEMETRY=1
L278:     bend version
L279:     mkdir -p build
L280:     bend tests.bend -o build/tests
L281:     ./build/tests --threads 2 --gpu off
L282:     bend gpu_tests.bend -o build/gpu_tests        # needs a Vulkan GPU, no display
L283:     ./build/gpu_tests --threads 2 --gpu off
L284: Open the quad example (colored quads and a texture made in Bend):
L285: 
L286:     bend examples/quads.bend -o build/quads
L287:     ./build/quads --threads 2 --gpu off
L288: 
L289: Resize the window to watch the layout follow; close it normally (or press Escape). The program prints the device report, frames presented, swapchain rebuilds and the teardown result.
L290: The Chromi example needs Chromi beside Voltra as well:
L291: 
L292:     git clone https://github.com/amage-si/chromi.git ../Chromi
L293:     bend examples/chromi.bend -o build/chromi
L294:     ./build/chromi --threads 2 --gpu off          # texture mode
L295:     ./build/chromi leaves --threads 2 --gpu off   # one quad per quadtree leaf
L296: 
L297: Click to change the accent color, press M to switch modes, and press Escape or close the window to exit. `--gpu off` refers to Bend's `!` compute offload, which Voltra does not use.
L298: ## Using it
L299: 
L300:     `import Base
L301:     import ./Voltra/gpu.bend as V
L302:     import ./Voltra/quads.bend as Q
L303:     import ./Ankra/window.bend as A
L304: 
L305:     def main() -> IO(Unit):
L306:       do IO<Unit>:
L307:         +win : A.Win <- IO.try(A.Win, A.open(A.options("Hello", 640, 400)))
L308:         +native : List<&2, U32> <- A.native(win)
L309:         +g : V.Gpu <- V.open(native, 640, 400, True{})
L310:         +g1 : V.Gpu <- V.draw(g, [Q.rounded(320, 320, 1920, 1280, 96, 4282664191)], 255)
L311:         got : A.Win & List<&2, A.Input> <- A.wait(win, 2000)
L312:         +report : V.Report <- V.close(g1)
L313:         IO.print(V.report.show(report))
L314:         +left : U32 <- A.close(win)
L315:         IO.print("window objects left: " ++ U32.show(left))
L316:     `
L317: The context is a value: every call returns the next `Gpu`. Colors are straight RGBA8 packed `0xRRGGBBAA`; coordinates are physical pixels from the top left (rounded boxes in 1/8 pixels). Close Voltra before the window. Read the cite119†API reference , the cite120†bridge reference and the cite121†examples .
L318: ## The native bridge
L319: `native/voltra.c` (1,940 lines, 1,556 non-blank and non-comment), with the JS twin Bend requires (`native/voltra.js`, which answers ENOTSUP), exposes 38 effects. Each one is a single Vulkan call, or a field-by-field translation of Bend words into one Vulkan create-info struct; `vk_record` translates each of 15 command words into one `vkCmd*` call. Objects cross into Bend as `U32` slot ids.
L320: Bend decides everything else: which GPU, queue family, memory type, format, present mode and image count; when to rebuild the swapchain; barriers, layouts and command order; frames in flight; atlas placement; and the order in which objects are destroyed.
L321: Vulkan is loaded with `dlopen("libvulkan.so.1")`, and the bridge declares the Vulkan types it uses, checked against the Khronos headers by `native/abi_check.py`. Shaders are GLSL compiled to SPIR-V by `shaders/build.sh`; the SPIR-V and its Bend embedding are checked in.
L322: ## Current boundaries
L323:   * Linux with an Xlib surface (XWayland under Wayland compositors). Native Wayland surfaces, other platforms and multiple windows are not implemented.
L324:   * One Vulkan instance per process and one texture per context (an atlas is one texture). There is no mipmapping, depth buffer, MSAA, custom shader or user pipeline yet; images are sampled by nearest texel.
L325:   * `upload`, `update` and `read` are synchronous: they wait for the GPU to finish in-flight frames (`paint`'s regions do not).
L326:   * A partial frame redraws only its rectangles but still copies the whole canvas into the swapchain image (a GPU copy of the window, about 2 MB at 900x560); the present names only the changed rectangles.
L327:   * Hard failures (a Vulkan error, no usable GPU) end the program with the driver's message instead of returning an error value.
L328:   * Under FIFO on XWayland, drawing back to back is not held to the refresh rate (180-218 frames a second measured on this 120 Hz panel). Animation is paced by Ankra's loop instead (a timed grid of the monitor's refresh period: 120 frames a second, p99 interval 9.6 ms, none dropped; see cite122†docs/bench.md ). No vblank feedback is available on XWayland: present_wait completes at once there.
L329:   * Pixel-exact blending was verified on one GPU and driver; other drivers may round the blend differently (Vulkan only says they should round to nearest).
L330:   * The Khronos validation layer was not installed during development; only driver messages through `VK_EXT_debug_utils` were observed (none).
L331:   * Bend's checker reports `SOME PROOFS FAIL` for every def that reaches the foreign effects. That is expected: foreign code is outside Bend's proofs.

# Model the Domain

Encode the real domain in a data structure instead of scattering it across conditionals.

**Why:** Scattered booleans, repeated shape assumptions, and branching spread across files are accidental complexity. A structure that matches the domain makes invalid states unrepresentable and deletes branches. Choosing it at write time is cheap. Recovering it later reads as a refactor and gets deferred.

**Reach for structures like these:**

- A state machine instead of scattered booleans, phases, or lifecycle checks.
- A typed object/model instead of loose parameters or repeated shape assumptions.
- A map, registry, lookup table, or discriminated union instead of branching spread across files.
- A reducer or command/event model instead of ad hoc state mutations.
- A module organized around one body of domain knowledge instead of a sequence such as load, validate, transform, and save. Execution order is not ownership.
- A small module boundary that gathers repeated behavior, ownership, or invariants.
- A queue, cache, index, graph/tree, or normalized collection where the data access pattern calls for it.
- Any other structure that fits. When none fits, work out what the code must never allow and how the data gets read, then find the structure that encodes exactly that.

Do not force an abstraction. Prefer boring code if the current shape is already clear, local, and unlikely to grow. Be skeptical of an abstraction that adds indirection without removing branches, duplicated rules, invalid states, or lifecycle risk.

The sign that you skipped this is a new feature that grows an existing if/else chain by one more branch, or a second boolean that must stay in sync with the first. Temporal decomposition is another sign. Phase-named modules repeat the same domain rules across steps.
---
name: principle-boundary-discipline
description: "Apply when wiring validation, error handling, or framework adapters. Concentrate guards at system boundaries (CLI, config, network, external APIs); trust internal types and keep business logic in pure functions."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Boundary Discipline

Place validation, type narrowing, and error handling at system boundaries. Trust internal code unconditionally. Business logic lives in pure functions. The shell is thin and mechanical.

**Why:** Scattered validation is noisy, redundant, and gives a false sense of safety. Keep logic out of framework wiring so it can be tested without the framework.

**The pattern:**
- **At boundaries** (CLI args, config files, external APIs, network protocols): validate, return errors, handle defensively.
- **Inside the system:** typed data, error propagation, no re-validation. Trust the types.
- **Across the boundary.** Expose domain concepts, not the boundary's private representation. Keep general-purpose mechanism inside and special-purpose policy at the edge.

**Applications:**

Validation and error handling:
- Validate config at parse time (the boundary), not inside business logic
- Parse raw data into domain types at the boundary
- Do not re-export transport, storage, framework, or wire types through the public surface
- No redundant nil checks deep in call chains if the boundary already validated

Code organization:
- Business logic in pure functions with no framework dependencies
- Parse functions: pure transforms from raw bytes to typed state
- Prompt construction: structured state in, string out
- Scoring and assessment: pure transforms from state to results

**The tests:**
- "Is this data crossing a system boundary right now?" If not, validation is redundant.
- "Can this be a pure function that the shell just calls?" If yes, extract it.

# Voltra: instructions for contributors and agents

Voltra is the GPU layer of the AMAGE UI ecosystem, implemented in **Bend 2**:
devices, presentation surfaces, swapchains, buffers, textures, pipelines,
command submission and synchronization. Read the README for current
capabilities and limits; a roadmap item is not implemented merely because it
appears in the project scope.

## Implementation

- Implement library logic in Bend 2. Do not wrap an existing renderer or
  toolkit (wgpu, SDL, bgfx, raylib, ...).
- The native bridge (`native/voltra.c` and its JS twin) stays thin and
  explicit: one effect per Vulkan call, or a field-by-field translation of
  Bend words into one Vulkan struct. Decisions belong in Bend: device and
  memory selection, formats, present modes, resize policy, barriers and
  layouts, command order, frames in flight, atlas placement, lifetimes and
  destruction order. If a new native call is needed, add the smallest one,
  document it in `docs/bridge.md`, and keep `native/abi_check.py` passing.
- Windows and their events belong to Ankra: Voltra makes its surface from the
  native window Ankra hands over and never opens a window or reads events.
- The shader's integer rules are a contract with Chromi's CPU reference
  (`Chromi/replay.bend`): change both together and keep `gpu_tests.bend`
  and Chromi's `gpu_tests.bend` at 0 differing pixels.
- The official Bend compiler/runtime, the OS, the Vulkan loader and the
  driver remain external dependencies.
- Before writing Bend, run `bend version` and read `bend guide` (and
  `bend guide effects` for the bridge) from the installed toolchain. Verify
  syntax and runtime internals instead of assuming older examples still work.
- Keep source, comments, documentation and commit messages in English.

## Writing fast Bend

Correct Bend is not fast Bend by default. Measured rules (Bend 2.0.35):

- Indexed, large or hot data (bytes, pixels, coverage, quads) lives in an
  `Array<U32>` (native flat block, ~1 ns/read), not a `List`. Lists are fine
  when tiny, built once and consumed in order. Arrays are affine and cannot be
  fields of `Data` types: keep them local and convert once at the boundary.
- No `do Result`/`do Maybe` binds or callbacks per byte, pixel or glyph: each
  bind is a closure (45% of a measured profile). Thread state through one
  recursive def that matches on the result.
- `||`, `&&` and `Bool.pick` evaluate both sides; use `match` to stop early.
- Never `Array.clone` or append (`List.append`) in a loop; build with a
  reversed accumulator or a tail parameter.
- A parameter that a def only matches or passes to itself is borrowed (no
  refcount); descend trees with the selector as a parameter.
- Keep non-recursive records small (they are passed flattened; the widest one
  widens every call frame). Box big ones with an `Alias{x: T}` constructor.
- Split independent, balanced work of tens of µs or more with a parallel call
  (`a b = f(l) g(r)`); never parallelize tiny or IO-bound work.
- Measure before and after on the same input; print a result before the next
  `IO.now()`.

Here: quads and texels reach the GPU as flat arrays (`Q.put`, `Q.words`,
`region_words`); keep new upload and draw paths that way. Quads that stay
the same between frames belong in the store (`store`, `C.Spans` runs), not
in words sent again every frame. Region pixels are still a `List` field
(`Region` is `Data`), written straight into the array once.

## Linux first

The initial goal is excellent behavior on the actual Linux development
machine: correctness, stability, measured performance and a finished user
experience. Inspect the effective environment (driver, loader, layers,
compositor) before choosing integrations.

Build compatibility layers as the project progresses, after visible,
well-made Linux results. Do not let speculative platform abstractions delay
local quality. Introduce abstractions from concrete needs.

## Working practice

- Preserve existing work and keep the library's boundary clear: drawing
  belongs to Chromi, windows and input policy to Ankra.
- Favor simple, maintainable code. Back performance claims with measurements.
- Run the native checks after changes, and `gpu_tests.bend` when drawing
  changes. When presentation changes, run an example on a real window,
  capture only that window (its toplevel, never a screen region), check
  resize and normal closure, and confirm the teardown report (0 objects
  left, 0 driver messages).
- Compilation is not visual proof; a passing check is not proof of the whole
  system. State partial support and unverified behavior explicitly.
- Build sequentially and keep compilation units small; the Bend compiler can
  exhaust memory on large import graphs. Do not impose virtual-address limits
  on the Bend runtime or suppress crash reporting. Investigate failures
  before retrying.
- Keep generated binaries, logs, crash dumps, credentials and machine-specific
  evidence out of Git. Stage explicit paths and preserve concurrent changes.

# Foundational Thinking

**Structural decisions** protect option value. **Code-level decisions** protect simplicity.

**Data structures first.** Get the data shape right before writing logic. Define core types early, trace every access pattern, and choose structures that match the dominant paths.

At code level, DRY the structure, not every line. Types and data models should converge. Three similar statements still beat a premature abstraction. Prefer explicit over clever. Test behavior and edge cases, not line counts.

**Concurrency corollary.** Before sharing state between actors, ask "what happens if another actor modifies this concurrently?" If not "nothing", isolate.

**Scaffold first.** If something helps every later phase, do it first. Ask "does every subsequent phase benefit from this existing?" CI, linting, test infrastructure, and shared types are scaffold. Sequence for option value: setup before features, tests before fixes. Keep commits small and single-purpose.

Each increment should land a coherent abstraction or deepen one that exists. Do not spread a new capability across callers as special-case coordination.

Subtraction comes before scaffolding. Remove dead code first, then lay foundations.
---
name: principle-type-system-discipline
description: "Apply when designing types, reviewing a function signature, or writing code in any statically-typed language. Make illegal states unrepresentable, brand semantic primitives, parse external data at boundaries, refuse to lie to the compiler, exhaust variants, derive from authoritative schemas."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Type System Discipline

The type checker is a proof assistant. Use it to eliminate impossible states, mismatched primitives, and unhandled variants at compile time. A case the types let you ignore becomes a runtime failure the compiler could have stopped. Prefer defining errors and special cases out of existence over proliferating handlers. Unrepresentable states, total functions, and interface redesign (the patterns below) are the tools.

Applies to any typed language. Skills like `typescript-best-practices` ground it in specific syntax.

**The patterns:**

- **Make illegal states unrepresentable.** Model variants as sum types: discriminated unions in TypeScript, enums with payloads in Rust/Swift/Kotlin, sealed classes in Scala, ADTs in Haskell/OCaml. Don't model state as a bag of optional fields where contradictory combinations compile. A subtle anti-pattern: `{ completed: boolean; completedAt?: Date }` admits `completed: true; completedAt: undefined`, which is meaningless. Derive the boolean from a single source like `completedAt !== null`, or model the variants explicitly as `{ kind: 'open' } | { kind: 'done'; at: Date }`. If a bug forces the question "wait, can this combination actually happen?", the type is too loose.
- **Types are constructions, not restrictions.** Build the type up from the values you want instead of carving them out of a looser type with checks. The invariant that seems to need a refinement type is usually a construction away. A non-empty list is a head plus a rest, not a list with a length check. A valid time range is a start plus a duration, not two timestamps you must keep ordered. No representation is privileged. A list of pairs is an even-length list if you interpret it that way, so choose the shape that cannot build the illegal value and expose the interface callers need on top.
- **Brand semantic primitives.** `UserId` and `OrderId` are strings underneath but should not be interchangeable. Newtypes in Rust, opaque types in Swift, value classes in Kotlin, phantom types in Haskell, branded intersections in TypeScript. Validate once at creation, trust the type downstream.
- **External data is untyped until parsed.** RPC payloads, JSON, IPC messages, CLI args, config files, environment variables, database rows. Have a parse function at every boundary that turns unstructured input into the typed model. See the **boundary-discipline** principle skill for where to put validation.
- **Don't lie to the type system.** Casts, unsafe coercions, and assertion functions that bypass the compiler are latent runtime crashes. If the compiler can't prove a fact, prove it (validate, narrow, refine the model) or accept that the cast is a hazard.
- **Exhaustive matching is the compiler's job.** When you match on a sum type, the compiler must fail compilation if a new variant is added without handling. Use the idiom your language provides: `never`-typed binding in TypeScript, unannotated `match` in Rust, `-Wincomplete-patterns` in Haskell, sealed-class match exhaustiveness in Kotlin.
- **Derive types from authoritative schemas.** When a protocol buffer, OpenAPI spec, GraphQL schema, database migration, or design-system token file defines a shape, derive from it instead of hand-rolling a parallel type. See the **encode-lessons-in-structure** principle skill.
- **Strengthen a type only where partiality appears.** A runtime assertion, null check, or "this should never happen" throw marks the place a type is too weak. Push that check up into the type. Then stop. The type system's job is to track the cases each use site must handle, not to describe the data as precisely as possible. Prefer total functions. `sum` of an empty list is 0, so it takes the plain list. `head` of an empty list has no answer, so it demands the non-empty one.

**The tests:**

- "Can I write a comment explaining when this combination of fields is valid?" If yes, the type is too loose. Split it into a sum type.
- "Do two of my function arguments share a primitive type but mean different things?" Brand them.
- "Where did this `any`, this `as`, this `assertNotNull` come from?" Trace it to the boundary and validate there instead.
- "If a new variant is added next month, will the compiler tell the next agent where to add a case?" If no, the match isn't exhaustive.
- "Is this type duplicating a shape another file owns?" Derive instead.
- "Am I strengthening this type to keep an operation total, or just to be more precise?" If nothing would otherwise panic, keep the plain type.
